exercises.name: Goblet squat
exercises.summary: A squat holding one dumbbell or kettlebell against your chest: your squat teacher in [[phase:p0]] and [[phase:p1]]. The load in front lets you sit deep with heels down and torso upright, and a failed rep simply ends with you putting the bell down. When the heaviest bell you can hold becomes the limit, move on to the [[ex:back-squat]] in [[phase:p2]].
setup: Take the bell from the rack, not the floor, and hold it upright against your breastbone (dumbbell by its top plate, kettlebell by the horns), elbows down.
Heels about shoulder-width apart, toes out 15-30 degrees, flat firm shoes rather than soft running shoes (practical convention).
execution: Sit straight down between your heels over 2-3 s, knees tracking forward and out over your toes.
Go to the deepest point you can hold with heels flat and lower back neutral; you passed the deep-squat screen, so aim for thighs below parallel.
Pause 1 s without relaxing, then stand up in 1-2 s with the bell still on your chest.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in and [[term:bracing|brace]] at the top, hold it through the bottom, breathe out on the way up. Take a fresh breath every rep.
cues: Keep the bell glued to your breastbone.
Spread the floor apart with your feet.
Sit down between your heels, as if onto a low stool.
Push the floor away to stand.

errors.error: Heels lift at the bottom.
errors.fix: Turn the toes out a little more, add [[ex:wu-ankle-rock]] to the warm-up, and stop just above that depth for now.

errors.error: Lower back rounds and the pelvis tucks under at the bottom.
errors.fix: Film a set from the side and stop just above the point where it starts; depth usually returns with practice.

errors.error: Knees cave in on the way up.
errors.fix: Use a lighter bell and think 'spread the floor' until the knees track over the toes every rep.

exercises.startingLoad: 10 bodyweight squats, then a 10-12 kg dumbbell. Add 2-2.5 kg per set until 10 reps leave 3-4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; that is your working weight.
exercises.effort: [[phase:p0]]: about 4 RIR, because you are practising the pattern. [[phase:p1]]: 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2, then 2-3 RIR ([[term:rpe|RPE]] 7-8). Never to failure: your grip on the bell and your technique give out before your legs ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]): when all sets reach 12 clean reps at the target RIR, go up one dumbbell step and rebuild from 8. When holding the bell, not your legs, ends the set, you are ready for the [[ex:back-squat]].
exercises.regression: Squat to a box at the depth you control, or do the unloaded [[ex:wu-bw-squat]] holding a rack upright.

alternatives.why: Same main muscles without the balance, grip or upper-back demand.
Single-leg squat pattern that also trains your weaker left leg on its own.
The loaded progression from Phase 2, inside a rack with safety arms.

exercises.whyChosen: You are new to loaded squatting and train alone. The goblet squat teaches depth, knee tracking and bracing with a load you can put down at any moment, with no rack or spotter, in line with [[dec:D08]]. Depth is worth learning early because, in a small trial, full squats grew the glutes and adductors more than half squats.
exercises.safety: If a rep stalls, sit onto your heels and set the bell on the floor. You train about an hour after waking, so make the first set extra easy (inference; see [[term:sleep-inertia|sleep inertia]]). Sharp knee or hip pain, as opposed to muscular effort, means stop and follow [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: Hips and knees extend together, so the quadriceps and gluteus maximus share the work and are stretched most at the bottom. Rectus femoris also crosses the hip and barely changes length in a squat, because the hip flexes as the knee bends, which is why the plan later adds the [[ex:leg-extension]] (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: Full squats grew gluteus maximus (+6.7% vs +2.2%) and adductors (+6.2% vs +2.7%) more than half squats over 10 weeks; neither depth grew rectus femoris or the hamstrings [@Kubo2019_squatDepth]. Full [[term:rom|range of motion]] gave more lower-limb [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] than partial range (ES 0.88) [@Pallares2021_ROMmeta]. In a small trial (n=30), reviewing video of your own squats after each set, with a physiotherapist pointing out the faults to fix, improved knee position and trunk lean versus no feedback [@Shin2023_videoFeedbackSquat]; review without expert guidance was not tested, so film one set from the side each session and check it against the errors listed here (inference). Cues about the movement's effect beat body-part cues for learning (retention g 0.58) [@Chua2021_externalFocusMA]. The goblet squat as the teaching variant is practical convention, not tested.

exercises.name: Barbell back squat (high bar)
exercises.summary: The main squat on Lower A from [[phase:p2]] to [[phase:p4]], with reps set by each block. The bar sits on your upper back, so your legs, not your arms, limit the load. Training alone makes three rules fixed: [[term:safety-arms|safety arms]] on every set, practise the bail before you load the bar, and never grind a rep.
setup: In a power rack, squat to depth with the empty bar and set the safety arms one hole (2-5 cm) below the bar's lowest point; set the hooks at about armpit height.
Grip just outside shoulder width and rest the bar on the muscle of your upper trapezius, not the neck bone; elbows pulled down.
Unrack, take two or three short steps back and set your feet as for the goblet squat. Use collars.
execution: Brace, then sit down between your heels over 2-3 s, the bar staying over your mid-foot.
Reach the depth you owned in the goblet squat (thighs below parallel, heels down, back neutral), with no bounce.
Drive up in 1-2 s with hips and chest rising together; breathe and re-brace at the top. To rack, walk forward until the bar touches the uprights, then bend the knees.
exercises.breathing: Take a full breath into your belly and brace before each rep, hold it through the bottom and breathe out near the top. This brief [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]] is normal on heavy reps; do not hold it across several reps.
cues: Bend the bar across your back.
Spread the floor apart.
Drive your upper back into the bar out of the bottom.
Keep the bar moving straight up over your mid-foot.

errors.error: Hips rise first and the squat turns into a forward lean.
errors.fix: Take about 10% off and drive your upper back into the bar as you leave the bottom.

errors.error: Depth shrinks as the load rises.
errors.fix: Film heavy sets from the side; reps short of your depth do not count towards progression.

errors.error: The bar sits on your neck or your wrists bend back.
errors.fix: Narrow the grip slightly and point the elbows down so the bar rests on muscle, not on your hands.

exercises.startingLoad: Empty bar for two sets of 8 (usually 20 kg; some gyms also have lighter technique bars, so check and note which you use). Add 10 kg per [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up set]] until the block's reps would leave 3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]], and hold that load for two sessions while technique settles.
exercises.effort: Every set at 2-3 RIR, the plan's target for free-weight compounds. End the set when a rep slows sharply. Never go to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] alone, even with safety arms ([[dec:D07]], [[dec:D15]]).
exercises.progression: When every set reaches the block's reps at the target RIR, add 2.5-5 kg ([[rule:double-progression]]). Estimate strength with [[tool:e1rm]] rather than testing a true [[term:1rm|1RM]] alone; for stalls, follow [[rule:stall]].
exercises.regression: Return to the [[ex:goblet-squat]] for a technique reset, or run the [[ex:hack-squat]] or [[ex:leg-press]] as the main lift for a cycle (allowed in [[phase:p4]]).

alternatives.why: Guided machine squat you can push closer to failure safely alone.
Same leg work with no bar on your back; first choice when your back is sore.
Technique reset with a load you can simply put down.

exercises.whyChosen: A deep loaded squat trains the quadriceps, glutes and adductors together and builds strength that probably carries over to hiking and sport (inference). Inside a rack with safety arms, the main hazard of training alone, being pinned under the bar, is managed. High bar keeps your torso upright, close to the goblet squat you learned (practical convention).
exercises.safety: **Practise the bail before your first loaded set**: with the empty bar, squat to the bottom, sit a little lower so the bar settles on the safety arms, then slide out backwards. Two-thirds of weight-training injuries seen in emergency departments came from a weight dropping on the person, and 90% involved free weights [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]; safety arms are the countermeasure (inference, not trial-tested). At 13:00, an hour after waking, add one extra ramp-up set ([[rule:ramp-up]]).
exercises.mechanism: The joint actions match the goblet squat, but with the bar on your back the hip and knee extensors and the adductor magnus can work to their own limit rather than your arms' limit. At full depth the glutes and adductors are lengthened under high torque, probably the source of the extra growth from deep squats (inference).
exercises.evidence: Full squats grew the glutes (+6.7% vs +2.2%) and adductors more than half squats and raised full-squat 1RM more (+31.8% vs +11.3%) [@Kubo2019_squatDepth]. Squats grew the quadriceps (+3.6 cm²) and adductors (+2.5 cm²) more than hip thrusts, with similar glute growth [@Plotkin2023_hipThrustVsSquat]. In trained men, 3-min rests beat 1-min rests for squat 1RM and thigh thickness [@Schoenfeld2016_rest_RCT], hence the 180 s. People underestimate the reps they have left by about one on average [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy], and in a tiny study (n=16), lifters with under 18 months of training judged Smith-machine squat RIR as accurately as more experienced lifters [@Droguett2025_RIRnoviceSquat]; complete beginners were not tested.

exercises.name: Hack squat (machine)
exercises.summary: A squat on an angled sled, with pads on your shoulders and your back against a pad. It has no fixed slot in the plan: use it in place of the [[ex:back-squat]] when you want to push close to failure alone, or as the [[phase:p4]] main lift for a cycle.
setup: Set the shoulder pads so you start with the knees slightly bent; feet mid-platform, shoulder-width, toes slightly out.
Check where the safety catch stops the sled before you load it, and release the safety handles only once you are in position.
execution: Lower over 2-3 s, knees travelling forward over the toes, back and hips flat on the pad.
Go as deep as you can before your hips peel off the pad or your heels lift, usually thighs at or below parallel to the platform.
Drive up in 1-2 s through the whole foot and stop just short of locking the knees; re-engage the handles after the last rep.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in and brace at the top, breathe out through the upper half of each rep; keep breath-holds brief on the last hard reps.
cues: Push the platform through the floor.
Keep your back pinned to the pad.
Spread the platform apart with your feet.

errors.error: Hips peel off the back pad at the bottom.
errors.fix: Stop a little higher, or place your feet slightly higher on the platform.

errors.error: Heels lift off the platform.
errors.fix: Move your feet higher on the platform.

errors.error: Knees slam into lockout.
errors.fix: Stop a few degrees short of straight to keep the load on the muscles.

exercises.startingLoad: Machines differ widely in sled weight and leverage. Start with the empty sled for 10 reps, then add 5 kg per side per set until the target reps leave 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. Name the machine in your Hevy notes, because loads do not transfer between brands.
exercises.effort: Most sets at 1-2 RIR; the last set may go to 0 RIR because the sled cannot pin you. [[term:momentary-failure|Failure]] is allowed here, not required ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]]: when all sets reach the top of the rep range at the target RIR, add 5-10 kg.
exercises.regression: The [[ex:leg-press]], or a shallower range you fully control.

alternatives.why: Even more supported, and found in almost every gym.
The free-weight version, for strength that transfers to barbell lifts.
When the machine is busy or your gym has none.

exercises.whyChosen: It keeps a deep, quadriceps-heavy squat while removing the balance and bail-out problems of a barbell, which matters when nobody can spot you. Machines and free weights build muscle similarly (see evidence).
exercises.safety: Before the first work set, check where the catch would stop the sled if you sat down under it; if it would trap you below your depth, keep 2 RIR on every set. Never step out with the safety handles released.
exercises.mechanism: The back pad and rails stop your torso pitching forward, so the knees travel further forward and the knee extensors take a larger share of the work than in a free squat (biomechanical reasoning; not measured in the catalogued trials).
exercises.evidence: Free-weight and machine training produced similar hypertrophy (SMD -0.06) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], and similar quadriceps growth in a direct trial (differences of 2% or less) [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT]. In 18 trained lifters, stopping 1-2 reps short of failure grew the quadriceps as much as training to failure (+0.18 cm in both) [@Refalo2024_FAILvsRIRhypertrophy]. No catalogued trial tested the hack squat itself.

exercises.name: Leg press (deep)
exercises.summary: You push a sled away with your legs from a seated or reclined position. With rails and safety stops, it is the lower-body exercise you can push closest to failure alone, so it runs through every phase: technique session A ([[phase:p0]]), Full body B ([[phase:p1]]), Lower B ([[phase:p2]] to [[phase:p4]], from week 17 in Phase 3) and the main lift of maintenance session A ([[phase:pm]]).
setup: Sit fully back with your lower back against the pad; feet mid-platform, shoulder-width, toes slightly out.
With the empty sled, find your deepest position before the pelvis curls off the pad, and set the safety stops just below it.
execution: Release the handles and lower the sled over 2-3 s, knees moving towards your chest in line with your toes.
Stop at your depth, usually with the knees bent to 90 degrees or more, without bouncing off the bottom.
Push the platform away in 1-2 s through your whole foot and stop just short of locking the knees.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in at the top, hold briefly through the bottom and breathe out through the second half of the push. Avoid long, straining breath-holds on the last reps (see safety).
cues: Push the platform through the wall.
Keep your hips pinned to the seat.
Leave a whole footprint on the platform.

errors.error: Pelvis rolls off the pad at the bottom (butt wink).
errors.fix: Shorten the range slightly or place your feet higher on the platform.

errors.error: Knees lock hard at the top.
errors.fix: Stop just short of straight on every rep.

errors.error: Knees cave in on heavy reps.
errors.fix: Reduce the load and keep the knees in line with the toes.

exercises.startingLoad: Empty sled for 10 reps, then add 10-20 kg per set until 10 reps leave 3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. In Hevy, log only the plates you add and name the machine in the notes, because sled weights differ (practical convention).
exercises.effort: [[phase:p0]]: about 4 RIR. [[phase:p1]] weeks 1-2: 3-4 RIR. From week 3: 1-2 RIR, with 0-1 RIR allowed on the last set because the sled cannot trap you. As the main lift of maintenance mode ([[phase:pm]]): 2-3 RIR. Failure adds little growth but more discomfort (see evidence), so use it sparingly ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]] within the prescribed range (10-15, or 8-12 in maintenance): when all sets reach the top, add 5-10 kg.
exercises.regression: A shorter range you control with your pelvis on the pad, or a lighter load with a 3 s lowering.

alternatives.why: Similar machine stimulus with a more upright squat path.
Free-weight option when the leg press is taken.
Single-leg quadriceps and glute work without a machine.

exercises.whyChosen: A review of time-efficient training places a leg press or squat at the core of any short programme [@Iversen2021_time_efficient]. The leg press delivers that stimulus with the lowest skill and safety demands, and machines probably grow muscle about as well as free weights do (5 hypertrophy studies, wide confidence interval) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta].
exercises.safety: Keep the safety stops set and never push on your knees with your hands. In five experienced bodybuilders, directly measured blood pressure during double-leg presses to failure peaked at a mean of 320/250 mmHg [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting]; such peaks are brief, and resistance training is judged safe for adults with and without heart disease [@Paluch2023_AHAresistanceTraining], but stop for chest pain, a severe headache or dizziness ([[plan:safety]]).
exercises.mechanism: With your back supported, your legs rather than your balance or trunk limit the set. Deeper knee and hip flexion lengthens the quadriceps and gluteus maximus at the bottom, the range that full-range data favour (inference from squat trials).
exercises.evidence: Full [[term:rom|range of motion]] produced larger lower-limb growth than partial range (ES 0.88) [@Pallares2021_ROMmeta]. In 18 trained lifters, stopping 1-2 reps short of failure grew the quadriceps as much as failure (+0.18 cm in both) [@Refalo2024_FAILvsRIRhypertrophy] and, in a leg press and leg extension trial, felt less unpleasant (session RPE 4.3 vs 5.4) [@Refalo2025_proximityPerceptual].

exercises.name: Split squat (dumbbells)
exercises.summary: A stationary lunge: feet split front to back, you lower straight down and stand back up. It is your first [[term:unilateral|unilateral]] leg exercise (technique session B in [[phase:p0]], Full body B from week 3 of [[phase:p1]]). Every set starts with the left leg, which balanced worse at baseline (20 vs 30 s), and the right leg then matches its reps ([[dec:D28]]).
setup: From standing, step the left foot one long stride forward with feet hip-width apart side to side (two rails, not a tightrope); rear heel up.
Use bodyweight first, holding a rack upright with one hand if you wobble; later hold a dumbbell in each hand, arms straight.
execution: Lower straight down over about 2 s until your rear knee is just above the floor, front heel staying down.
Pause 1 s, then drive up through the whole front foot in 1-2 s to nearly straight knees.
Do all reps on the left, then the same number on the right, even if the right could do more.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in at the top and out as you rise; continuous breathing is fine at these loads.
cues: Drop straight down like a lift, not forward like an escalator.
Push the floor away with your front foot.
Let the dumbbells hang straight down beside your trouser seams.

errors.error: Feet in one line, so you wobble.
errors.fix: Widen the stance side to side to hip-width.

errors.error: Pushing up mainly off the back foot.
errors.fix: Keep most of your weight on the front foot; the back foot only balances you.

errors.error: Front heel lifts at the bottom.
errors.fix: Lengthen the stance until the heel stays down.

exercises.startingLoad: Bodyweight in [[phase:p0]] (8 per side). In [[phase:p1]], two 4-6 kg dumbbells, adding 2-2.5 kg per hand when the left leg reaches the top of the range.
exercises.effort: [[phase:p0]]: about 4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. [[phase:p1]] (from week 3): 2-3 RIR, judged on the left leg. Balance should never be what ends a set; if it is, hold a support.
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]]: when the left leg does 12 reps per set at 2 RIR with steady balance, add load; then drop the hand support; then move to the [[ex:bulgarian-split-squat]] in [[phase:p2]].
exercises.regression: Hold a rack upright, shorten the range (rear knee to a folded mat), or return to bodyweight.

alternatives.why: Adds a step on every rep and more balance demand.
Less knee bend under load; closest to uphill hiking.
The harder progression with the rear foot raised.

exercises.whyChosen: Unilateral training raises single-leg strength more than bilateral training, with similar muscle growth (see evidence), and lets you train and track the left-right difference directly. The split squat is the most stable unilateral option, which suits a beginner whose left leg balances worse.
exercises.safety: Keep a rack upright or bench within reach. If you lose balance, step out wide and let the dumbbells go to your sides rather than fighting for the rep (practical convention).
exercises.mechanism: The front leg performs a supported single-leg squat (quadriceps and gluteus maximus), while the hip abductors and adductors steady the pelvis on a narrow base, which is the link to balance (inference).
exercises.evidence: Unilateral training improved unilateral strength more than bilateral training (ES 0.65 in one meta-analysis, g 0.42 in another) and unilateral jumps (g 0.35), with no clear difference in hypertrophy [@Kassiano2025_uniVsBiMeta; @Xin2026_uniVsBiMultilevel]. Starting with the weaker side is practical convention: no catalogued trial tests whether it shrinks asymmetry.

exercises.name: Bulgarian split squat
exercises.summary: A split squat with your rear foot on a bench, which puts most of your weight on the front leg and lets it sink deeper. It is the unilateral exercise on Lower B in [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p4]] and in maintenance session B ([[phase:pm]]), 8-12 reps per side, left leg first.
setup: Stand in front of a stable bench at knee height or a little lower and rest the top of your right foot on it, laces down; pad the edge with a folded towel if it digs in.
Hop the left foot forward until, at the bottom, your front shin is roughly vertical to slightly forward. Hold a dumbbell in each hand.
execution: Lower straight down over 2-3 s until the front thigh is about parallel to the floor or the rear knee is close to it.
Pick a torso angle and keep it so your logs compare: a slight forward lean shifts work to the glutes, staying upright shifts it to the quadriceps.
Drive up through the front foot in 1-2 s. Finish all left reps, then switch and match them on the right.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in at the top and out as you rise; brace briefly on the heaviest sets.
cues: Sink straight down between the bench and your front foot.
Push the floor away with your front foot.
Keep the dumbbells hanging close to your front foot.

errors.error: Stance too short: the front heel lifts and the knee feels jammed.
errors.fix: Move the front foot further from the bench.

errors.error: Stance too long: a strong pull at the front of the rear hip and little depth.
errors.fix: Bring the front foot closer to the bench.

errors.error: Pushing off the rear foot.
errors.fix: The rear foot only rests on the bench; the front leg does the work.

errors.error: Wobbling sideways.
errors.fix: Widen the stance side to side, or hold a rack upright with one hand and one dumbbell in the other.

exercises.startingLoad: First session at bodyweight. Then roughly two-thirds of the dumbbells you used for 12 [[ex:split-squat]] reps (practical convention), adjusted until the left leg's set ends at 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]].
exercises.effort: 2-3 RIR, judged on the left leg. It feels harder than the load suggests; end the set on rep quality and balance, not on discomfort ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]]: when the left leg completes 12 reps per set at 2 RIR, add 2-2.5 kg per hand. If your grip gives out before your legs, use straps or hold one heavier dumbbell at your chest.
exercises.regression: Back to the [[ex:split-squat]] with the rear foot on the floor, or hold a support.

alternatives.why: Same pattern with the rear foot on the floor; easier balance.
Unilateral option with a dynamic step.
Gentler on the knees and the rear hip; carries over to hiking.

exercises.whyChosen: It loads one leg close to its full capacity with modest dumbbells, so there is less weight to manage alone, and the deep hip flexion at the bottom works the glutes at long length. It also keeps the left-first rule of [[dec:D28]] in every lower-body week.
exercises.safety: Expect marked [[term:doms|delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)]] after the first sessions, so keep to 2 sets in the first week (practical convention). Unaccustomed exercise is a recognised cause of [[term:rhabdomyolysis|exertional rhabdomyolysis]] [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo]; it is rare, but very dark urine or severe swelling after a session needs same-day medical review ([[plan:safety]]).
exercises.mechanism: With most of your bodyweight on the front leg, its quadriceps and gluteus maximus work near single-leg capacity, and hip flexion at the bottom stretches the glute under load. Leaning forward increases hip flexion and the hip-extension demand; staying upright shifts work to the knee (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: Unilateral training improved single-leg strength more than bilateral training, with similar hypertrophy [@Kassiano2025_uniVsBiMeta; @Xin2026_uniVsBiMultilevel]. A narrative review argues for exercises that load muscles meaningfully in the lengthened position [@Pedrosa2026_muscleLengthReview], although a meta-analysis found only trivial regional differences between long and short training lengths [@Varovic2025_lengthRegionalMeta]. No catalogued trial tested the Bulgarian split squat itself.

exercises.name: Reverse lunge (dumbbells)
exercises.summary: You step one foot back into a lunge and return to standing. It is the unilateral exercise on Lower B in [[phase:p3]] (8-12 reps per side). The step and weight transfer on every rep challenge dynamic balance more than the [[ex:split-squat]] does.
setup: Stand tall, feet hip-width, a dumbbell in each hand, with at least a long stride of clear floor behind you.
'Left leg first' means the left foot stays planted and works while the right foot steps back.
execution: Shift your weight onto the left foot and step the right foot back a long stride, landing on the ball of the foot.
Lower over about 2 s until the rear knee is just above the floor, front shin near vertical, torso slightly forward.
Push through the front foot to bring the rear foot back beside it in 1-2 s and settle on both feet before the next rep. Finish all left reps, then switch.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in as you step back and out as you return to standing.
cues: Step back onto your own rail, hip-width out.
Push the floor away with your front foot.
Return to the same footprints every rep.

errors.error: The rear foot lands in line with the front foot, so you wobble.
errors.fix: Step back along a line hip-width to the side.

errors.error: Returning by pushing off the back foot.
errors.fix: Let the front leg pull you back up; the back foot only guides.

errors.error: Rushing reps and losing balance at the top.
errors.fix: Pause on both feet for one breath between reps.

exercises.startingLoad: One or two dumbbell steps (2-5 kg per hand) lighter than your recent split-squat working load, then adjust to 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]].
exercises.effort: 2-3 RIR, judged on the left leg; the right matches the left's reps. End the set when balance, rather than the legs, starts to fail.
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]]: when the left leg completes 12 reps per set at 2 RIR, add 2-2.5 kg per hand.
exercises.regression: The [[ex:split-squat]] (no step), a shorter step, or one hand on a rack upright.

alternatives.why: Same muscles without the step; easier balance.
More range and more load on the front leg.
Lower knee stress and close carry-over to hiking.

exercises.whyChosen: In [[phase:p3]] it replaces the Bulgarian split squat, changing the stimulus while keeping the target muscles; reasoned variation of this kind can help, whereas excessive random rotation may blunt gains (see evidence). Stepping backwards spares the front knee from braking your forward momentum, which tends to make it easier on the knee than a forward lunge (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.safety: Clear the floor behind you before each set. If you lose balance, put the rear foot down wider and let the dumbbells go to your sides.
exercises.mechanism: The planted leg lowers you (an [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] action) and drives you back up ([[term:concentric|concentric]]), while each step adds a weight transfer that the hip stabilisers and ankle must control, a [[term:proprioception|proprioception]] demand the split squat lacks (inference).
exercises.evidence: A systematic review concluded that anatomically reasoned exercise variation can enhance regional growth and strength, while excessive random rotation may blunt gains [@Kassiano2022_variationSR]. Unilateral training improved unilateral strength more than bilateral training (g 0.42) [@Xin2026_uniVsBiMultilevel]. In inactive students, a programme designed to feel more varied slightly improved adherence over 6 weeks [@Sylvester2015_varietySupportRCT].

exercises.name: Step-up (dumbbells)
exercises.summary: You step onto a knee-height box or bench and stand up on one leg. It has no fixed slot in the plan: it is the unilateral substitute when split squats or lunges bother your knees, or when you want leg work that resembles hiking uphill ([[rule:substitution]]).
setup: Use a stable box or bench about knee height that cannot slide or tip, with a dumbbell in each hand.
Place the whole left foot on the box; the right foot stays on the floor.
execution: Lean slightly forward and drive through the left foot to stand fully on the box in 1-2 s, bringing the right foot up beside it.
Step the right foot back down over 2-3 s, keeping the left foot on the box, and touch down lightly.
Finish all left reps, then switch.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you step up and in as you lower.
cues: Push the box down into the floor.
Let the trailing foot float; it is only along for the ride.
Touch the trailing foot down as quietly as you can.

errors.error: Bouncing up off the trailing foot.
errors.fix: Lift the trailing toes so the working leg has to do the lifting.

errors.error: The box is so high that your lower back rounds at the start.
errors.fix: Use a lower box (mid-shin to knee height).

errors.error: The knee caves inwards as you rise.
errors.fix: Use a lighter load and keep the knee over the middle of the foot.

exercises.startingLoad: Bodyweight for one session, then 4-8 kg dumbbells, adjusted to 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] at 8-12 reps per side.
exercises.effort: 2-3 RIR, judged on the left leg. End the set when you start pushing off the trailing foot.
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]] with load first; raise the box only if your pelvis stays level and your back neutral.
exercises.regression: A lower box, or one hand on a rack upright.

alternatives.why: More knee-bend range and more load for the quadriceps.
Similar muscles with a backwards step.

exercises.whyChosen: It trains the quadriceps and glutes on one leg with little knee bend under load and a direct link to uphill hiking and stairs, and strength carries over best to tasks that resemble the trained movement (see evidence).
exercises.safety: Never stack loose plates as a step, and keep the box out of the walkway around the dumbbell rack. Step down; do not jump down.
exercises.mechanism: Stepping up is mostly [[term:concentric|concentric]] work for the working leg, and the controlled step down adds an [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] phase. A higher box increases hip flexion and the demand on the glutes (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: Dynamic training improved strength in the trained task about twice as much as untrained isometric strength (SMD 0.98 vs 0.42) [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta], and unilateral training favoured unilateral strength (g 0.42) [@Xin2026_uniVsBiMultilevel]. No catalogued trial tested the step-up for hypertrophy.

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift (dumbbells)
exercises.summary: A [[term:hip-hinge|hip hinge]]: knees softly bent, you push your hips back and lower two dumbbells down the front of your legs, then drive the hips forward to stand. It is your hinge teacher and main free-weight hamstring exercise in technique session A ([[phase:p0]]), Full body A ([[phase:p1]], [[term:superset|superset]] C) and maintenance session A ([[phase:pm]]). Because you cannot touch your toes, your range will be shorter than in videos at first; it grows with training.
setup: Feet hip-width, a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs, palms facing you.
Unlock the knees to a soft bend (about 15-20 degrees) and keep that angle for the whole rep; brace lightly, ribs down.
execution: Push your hips back over about 3 s, sliding the dumbbells down the front of your thighs and keeping them close.
Stop when you feel a strong hamstring stretch or your lower back is about to round, whichever comes first; at first this may be around knee height.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall in 1-2 s, finishing with glutes tight and without leaning back.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in and brace at the top, hold as you lower, breathe out as you stand.
cues: Push your hips back to touch a wall behind you.
Slide the dumbbells down your trouser legs.
Drive your belt buckle forward to stand.

errors.error: Squatting it: the knees bend more as you go down.
errors.fix: Set the knee angle at the start and move only the hips back.

errors.error: Rounding the lower back to reach further.
errors.fix: Stop where the back starts to round; that is your current range.

errors.error: The dumbbells drift away from the legs.
errors.fix: Keep them brushing your thighs and shins on the way down and up.

errors.error: Leaning back at the top.
errors.fix: Finish tall with glutes tight and ribs down, body in a straight line.

exercises.startingLoad: Rehearse 10 reps holding a dowel or light bar, then two 6-8 kg dumbbells for 10 reps at 3-4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; add 2-2.5 kg per hand per set until you find your working weight.
exercises.effort: [[phase:p0]]: about 4 RIR. [[phase:p1]]: 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2, then 2-3 RIR; maintenance: 2-3 RIR. Your back position will usually fail before your hamstrings, so do not chase failure on a free-weight hinge ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]]: when all sets reach 12 reps with a neutral back, add 2-2.5 kg per hand. Let the range grow only as fast as your back stays neutral, and re-test with [[ex:test-ftf]] ([[dec:D27]]). When dumbbell handling or grip limits the set, move to the [[ex:bb-rdl]] in [[phase:p2]].
exercises.regression: A shorter range (to just above the knees), a dowel held along your spine (touching head, upper back and tailbone) to learn the hinge, or the [[ex:back-extension]].

alternatives.why: Heavier, more progressive version from Phase 2.
Same hinge with lower skill and no grip demand.
Hamstring work that bypasses the back entirely.

exercises.whyChosen: You need a hinge for daily lifting, hiking and later deadlift variants, and squats did not grow the hamstrings in a small trial (see evidence). The RDL loads the hamstrings and glutes while they are lengthened, and dumbbells let you learn with light loads you can set down at any point. Pairing it with another exercise in superset C saves session time ([[sci:sci-dose]]).
exercises.safety: You lift about an hour after waking. Some clinicians advise avoiding heavy end-range spinal flexion in the first hour after rising, when the discs are most hydrated (practical convention, not tested in the catalogued evidence); a neutral back and a full warm-up cover this. Some rounding under load has not been shown to cause back pain (see evidence), so if it happens, end the range there rather than worry. Pain that lingers after the session: [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: Three of the four hamstring heads cross both the hip and the knee. With the knees almost straight and the hips flexing, they are stretched under load, as are the gluteus maximus and adductor magnus. Your range is set by hamstring extensibility and [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]], which loaded training itself improves ([[sci:sci-flexibility]]).
exercises.evidence: No catalogued trial measured hamstring growth from Romanian deadlifts, so their inclusion is reasoned. Squats at either depth did not grow the hamstrings [@Kubo2019_squatDepth], and the hamstrings grew more when trained at longer lengths (seated vs lying curls, +14% vs +9%) [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl]. Resistance training improved range of motion (ES 0.73; ES 1.04 in untrained people) about as much as stretching did (no significant difference) [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM; @Afonso2021_STvsStretchMeta]. In low-quality evidence, lumbar flexion during lifting was not a risk factor for low back pain [@Saraceni2020_lumbarFlexionMeta].

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift (barbell)
exercises.summary: The barbell version of the [[ex:db-rdl]] and the main lift on Lower B from [[phase:p2]] (6-10 reps there, then the block's reps in [[phase:p3]] and [[phase:p4]]; in weeks 9-16 of Phase 3 the [[ex:trap-bar-deadlift]] takes its place). Every set starts standing, with the bar taken from the rack at mid-thigh, so you never pull from the floor with a rounded back.
setup: Inside a power rack, set the hooks at mid-thigh height and the safety arms just below the lowest point the bar reaches in your RDL.
Overhand grip just outside your thighs (add straps once grip limits); stand up with the bar, take one step back, feet hip-width, knees soft.
execution: Brace and push your hips back over about 3 s, the bar sliding down your thighs in contact with your legs.
Lower until the hamstring stretch is strong or your back is about to round, typically somewhere between the knee and mid-shin.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall in 1-2 s, and take a breath at the top between reps.
exercises.breathing: Take a full breath and brace before each rep, hold it during the descent, breathe out near the top and re-brace.
cues: Shave your thighs with the bar.
Push your hips back to the wall behind you.
Bend the bar around your legs.
Push the floor away as you stand.

errors.error: The bar drifts forward off the legs.
errors.fix: Keep it brushing the thighs; 'bend the bar around your legs' tightens the upper back.

errors.error: The knees bend more as the bar descends.
errors.fix: Hold the soft-knee angle you set at the top; the movement happens at the hips.

errors.error: The back rounds near the bottom on later reps.
errors.fix: End the range there; if it happens early in the set, take 5-10 kg off.

exercises.startingLoad: Empty bar for 10 reps. A reasonable first working estimate is the combined weight of the two dumbbells you finished [[phase:p1]] with, adjusted in 5-10 kg steps until 8 reps leave 3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] (practical convention).
exercises.effort: 2-3 RIR on every set. With 6-10 heavy reps, stop when bar speed drops noticeably or your back position changes; no grinding ([[dec:D07]], [[dec:D15]]).
exercises.progression: When all sets reach the top of the range at the target RIR, add 2.5-5 kg ([[rule:double-progression]]) and track strength with [[tool:e1rm]]. Use straps rather than letting your grip cap the hamstrings.
exercises.regression: The [[ex:db-rdl]] or a shorter range; on a sore-back day, swap in the [[ex:back-extension]] or [[ex:seated-leg-curl]].

alternatives.why: Lighter, easier to bail from and kinder to the grip.
Lower-skill hinge for the glutes and hamstrings.
Heavier hinge-squat hybrid for a strength block.

exercises.whyChosen: A barbell lets you load the hinge well beyond what dumbbells allow and keeps the load centred over your feet. Starting at mid-thigh avoids the floor pull, the position tight hamstrings find hardest to reach with a neutral back ([[dec:D27]]).
exercises.safety: Work inside the rack so you can lower the bar onto the safety arms if your grip or back gives out. In mostly retrospective studies, competitive bodybuilders reported low injury rates, roughly 0.24-1 per 1000 h, and across weight-training sports the commonest injuries were strains, tendinitis and sprains, often of the shoulder, lower back and knee [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury]. Add one ramp-up set at 13:00 ([[rule:ramp-up]]); the morning-disc caution in [[ex:db-rdl]] applies here too.
exercises.mechanism: As in the dumbbell version, the hip flexes with the knees nearly straight, so the biarticular hamstrings, gluteus maximus and adductor magnus lengthen under a high hip-extension torque. A heavier bar raises that torque at the bottom, where the muscles are longest (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: No catalogued trial measured hypertrophy from the RDL; it is included because squats did not grow the hamstrings [@Kubo2019_squatDepth] and longer-length hamstring training grew them more [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl]. Low-quality evidence found no link between lumbar flexion while lifting and low back pain [@Saraceni2020_lumbarFlexionMeta]. Rests longer than 2 min appear needed to maximise strength once trained [@Grgic2018_rest_strength], hence 150 s on this main lift.

exercises.name: Single-leg Romanian deadlift
exercises.summary: A Romanian deadlift on one leg: you hinge forward while the free leg extends behind you, joining a hamstring and glute hinge to single-leg balance. It has no fixed slot; use it in place of a unilateral exercise, or as a light hinge when you want balance work ([[dec:D28]]). Left side first, light load, hand support allowed early.
setup: To stand on the left leg, hold a light dumbbell in your right hand and rest your left hand on a rack upright or bench at first.
Keep the standing knee softly bent, about 15-20 degrees.
execution: Hinge forward at the left hip over about 3 s while the right leg extends straight behind you, torso and back leg moving as one line.
Lower until the hamstring stretch is strong or you can no longer keep your hips square to the floor.
Drive the left hip forward to stand in 1-2 s, touching the right toes down between reps only if you need to. Finish the left side, then the right.
exercises.breathing: Breathe steadily; exhale as you stand.
cues: Point your back heel at the wall behind you.
Keep your belt buckle facing the floor.
Push the floor away with your standing foot.

errors.error: Hips rotate open towards the free-leg side.
errors.fix: Point the back toes at the floor and keep the belt buckle square.

errors.error: The standing knee locks straight or bends into a squat.
errors.fix: Set a soft bend at the start and hold it.

errors.error: Rounding the back to reach lower.
errors.fix: End the range where your back would round; your hamstrings set it.

exercises.startingLoad: Bodyweight with hand support for the first session, then a 4-8 kg dumbbell, adjusted to 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] at 8-12 reps per side.
exercises.effort: 2-3 RIR, and end the set as soon as balance, rather than the muscle, limits a rep.
exercises.progression: Remove the hand support first, then add load, then lengthen the lowering to 4 s.
exercises.regression: The kickstand version (back toes resting lightly on the floor), full hand support, or the [[ex:bal-sl-reach]].

alternatives.why: Two-leg hinge that allows far more load.
Single-leg balance practice without the hinge load.
Unilateral leg work with more stability.

exercises.whyChosen: It trains the hinge and one-leg control together, which suits your balance gap (left 20 s vs right 30 s, eyes open). Doing the left first and matching the reps on the right follows [[dec:D28]] (practical convention).
exercises.safety: Keep a support within reach and the floor around you clear. Use your usual flat training shoes; a thick, soft sole makes balancing harder (practical convention).
exercises.mechanism: The standing hip flexes under load, so its hamstrings and glutes lengthen, while the hip abductors and rotators stop the pelvis tilting and rotating and the foot and ankle muscles keep you over your base, a [[term:proprioception|proprioception]] task (inference).
exercises.evidence: Unilateral training favoured unilateral strength (g 0.42) [@Xin2026_uniVsBiMultilevel], and hamstrings grew more when loaded at long lengths [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl]. Whether single-leg RDLs lengthen single-leg stance time has not been tested in the catalogued trials (inference).

exercises.name: Hip thrust (barbell or machine)
equipment: barbell with pad or hip-thrust machine
exercises.summary: With your upper back on a bench and a padded bar (or a machine belt) across your hips, you drive your hips up until your body is flat from knees to shoulders. It is optional glute work, programmed on Lower B in the first 16 weeks of [[phase:p3]] (8-12 reps). In one small trial it grew the glutes about as well as squats did, so you do not need it.
setup: Sit on the floor with the bench edge just below your shoulder blades; brace the bench against a rack or wall so it cannot slide.
Roll a bar with a thick pad to your hip crease, or set the machine belt across your hips. Feet flat and hip-width, placed so your shins are vertical at the top.
execution: Brace, tuck your chin slightly and drive through your heels to lift the hips in 1-2 s until torso and thighs form a straight line.
Hold the top for 1 s with ribs down; the rep ends when the hips are straight, not when the lower back arches.
Lower over about 2 s until the hips nearly touch the floor, then go again.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in at the bottom, brace, and breathe out at the top.
cues: Push the bar straight up to the ceiling.
Drive the floor away through your heels.
Keep your eyes on the wall in front of you, not the ceiling.

errors.error: Arching the lower back at the top instead of extending the hips.
errors.fix: Ribs down and chin tucked; stop when torso and thighs line up.

errors.error: Feet too close (the quadriceps take over) or too far (the hamstrings cramp).
errors.fix: Adjust until your shins are vertical at the top.

errors.error: The bench slides backwards.
errors.fix: Brace it against a rack or wall, or use the machine.

exercises.startingLoad: Empty bar with a pad for 12 reps, then add 10-20 kg per set until 8-12 reps leave 2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. Hip-thrust loads usually end up well above your squat loads for the same reps (practical convention).
exercises.effort: Barbell: 1-2 RIR, because rolling a heavy bar off your hips alone is awkward. Machine: 1-2 RIR, and the last set may reach failure ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]]: when all sets reach 12 reps, add 2.5-5 kg on the barbell, or the next step on a machine.
exercises.regression: The [[ex:wu-glute-bridge]] from the floor, or the machine version.

alternatives.why: Glute and hamstring work without setting up a bar.
Glutes and hamstrings at long length; already on Lower B.
Bodyweight version that needs no equipment.

exercises.whyChosen: It is easy to learn and loads the glutes heavily with little demand on the back or knees, which adds variety in [[phase:p3]]. Because squats grew the glutes about as much in a small trial, it stays optional rather than core ([[sci:sci-selection]]).
exercises.safety: Always use a thick bar pad. To get out from under the bar, lower your hips and roll the bar down your thighs; if a load is too heavy to roll off alone, use the machine instead (practical convention).
exercises.mechanism: The gluteus maximus is the main hip extensor. In the hip thrust the load is hardest near full hip extension, where the glute is short, which is the reverse of the squat, where it is loaded most when stretched (biomechanical reasoning). Higher muscle activity in the hip thrust did not translate into more growth (see evidence).
exercises.evidence: Over 9 weeks, hip thrusts and back squats grew gluteus maximus similarly (lower glutes -1.6 cm², 95% CI -6.1 to 2.0, slightly favouring the hip thrust), while squats grew the quadriceps (+3.6 cm²) and adductors (+2.5 cm²) more. Strength gains were specific to each lift, and the higher glute EMG during hip thrusts did not predict more growth [@Plotkin2023_hipThrustVsSquat].

exercises.name: 45-degree back extension (hip-dominant)
exercises.summary: On a 45-degree bench you hinge forward at the hips and come back up to a straight line. Done hip-dominant (spine held still, movement at the hips), it trains the glutes and hamstrings with low skill and no risk of being trapped. It has no fixed slot: use it in place of RDLs or hip thrusts, or to learn the hinge.
setup: Set the pad so its top edge sits just below your hip crease, leaving the hips free to fold over it.
Heels against the foot plate, feet hip-width, arms crossed over your chest.
execution: From a straight line, hinge at the hips and lower your torso over 2-3 s until the hamstring stretch is strong or your back starts to round.
Drive your hips into the pad to rise in 1-2 s to a straight line from head to heels, and stop there.
Keep the spine in one position throughout; the hips do the moving.
exercises.breathing: Breathe steadily: in on the way down, out on the way up.
cues: Drive your hips into the pad.
Reach the top of your head towards the far wall as you rise.
Stop when your body lines up with the bench.

errors.error: The pad is set too high, so the hips cannot fold and the spine bends instead.
errors.fix: Lower the pad to just below the hip crease.

errors.error: Arching past straight at the top.
errors.fix: Stop at a straight line; the extra arch adds back strain, not glute work.

errors.error: Rounding and unrounding the spine on every rep.
errors.fix: Hold the spine still and move only at the hips, with a shorter range if needed.

exercises.startingLoad: Bodyweight for 12-15 reps; then hold a 5-10 kg plate against your chest, and later a dumbbell.
exercises.effort: 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. Going to failure is safe on this bench, because you simply stop at the bottom.
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]] with plates in 2.5-5 kg steps; then add a 1 s pause at the bottom.
exercises.regression: A shorter range, or arms by your sides.

alternatives.why: Free-weight hinge with more load and carry-over.
Glute work with no back involvement.
Hamstrings without any hip hinge.

exercises.whyChosen: It is a low-skill hinge you can push hard alone, useful on days when your back is tired from heavier pulls or your grip is spent, and it rehearses the hips-not-spine pattern your RDLs need.
exercises.safety: Keeping the movement at the hips limits repeated loaded spinal bending. In a pig-spine model, tens of thousands of flexion-extension cycles under compression produced disc herniation [@Callaghan2001_porcineFlexion]; that is a very-low-certainty signal of unclear relevance to a few sets, but a reason to keep the spine still (inference). At 13:00, an hour after waking, start with an easy bodyweight set.
exercises.mechanism: With the knees straight and the hips flexing over the pad, the hamstrings and gluteus maximus lengthen under load in the lower part of the range, while the spinal erectors hold the spine rather than move it (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: No catalogued trial tested back extensions for hypertrophy, so inclusion rests on reasoning. Hamstrings grew more when trained at longer lengths [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl], and low-quality evidence found no link between lumbar flexion while lifting and low back pain [@Saraceni2020_lumbarFlexionMeta].

exercises.name: Seated leg curl
exercises.summary: A machine knee-flexion exercise done sitting: you curl a padded lever down and back under the seat. It is your main hamstring exercise in every phase, from technique session B ([[phase:p0]]) to Lower A in [[phase:p4]] (8-15 reps). It is chosen over the lying curl because sitting flexes the hip, which lengthens the hamstrings and grew them more in an MRI trial.
setup: Adjust the backrest so your knee joint lines up with the machine's pivot.
Lower the thigh pad firmly onto your thighs just above the knees, and set the lower pad against the back of your lower calves, just above the ankles.
Lean the torso slightly forward and hold the handles.
execution: Start with the knees almost straight, as far as the machine allows.
Curl the pad down and back in 1-2 s until your heels are under or behind your knees, and pause 1 s.
Return over 2-3 s to almost straight knees without letting the stack touch down between reps.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you curl and in as you return; no breath-holding.
cues: Pull the pad under the seat.
Drag your heels back towards the seat.
Keep the stack hovering between reps.

errors.error: The knee is not lined up with the pivot, so the pad rolls along your leg.
errors.fix: Move the backrest until the knee sits level with the axis.

errors.error: Hips lift off the seat to finish the rep.
errors.fix: Tighten the thigh pad and use a lighter load.

errors.error: Cutting the stretched end short.
errors.fix: Let the knees almost straighten on every rep; the long-length part is the point.

exercises.startingLoad: Machines vary. Start light (for example 15-25 kg on the stack) for 12 reps at about 4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] in [[phase:p0]], and go up one plate when you reach the top of the range.
exercises.effort: [[phase:p0]]: about 4 RIR. [[phase:p1]]: 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2, then 1-2 RIR. From [[phase:p2]]: 0-2 RIR, with failure acceptable on the last set because the machine cannot trap you ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]]: when all sets reach the top of the prescribed range, add one plate or the smallest add-on weight.
exercises.regression: A lighter load with a slower 3-4 s return, or the [[ex:lying-leg-curl]] if the seated machine does not fit you.

alternatives.why: When your gym has no seated curl; it still grows the hamstrings, somewhat less.
Hamstrings at long length through a hip hinge.
Glute and hamstring work on a simple bench.

exercises.whyChosen: Squats did not grow the hamstrings in a small trial, so they need direct knee-flexion work, and the seated position grew them more than lying (see evidence). With tight hamstrings, leaning forward increases the stretch, so lean only as far as is comfortable at first. In [[phase:p1]] it sits in [[term:superset|superset]] D to save time.
exercises.safety: Hamstring cramps near full contraction are common at first; if one starts, stop and gently straighten the knee (practical convention). A sharp, sudden pain at the back of the thigh, unlike a cramp, means stop and follow [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus and the long head of biceps femoris cross the hip as well as the knee. Flexing the hip (sitting, leaning forward) lengthens them, so the same knee curl happens at longer muscle lengths. The short head of biceps femoris crosses only the knee and grew equally in both positions, which fits this explanation.
exercises.evidence: Seated curls increased whole-hamstring MRI volume by 14% vs 9% for lying curls over 12 weeks, with the advantage in the biarticular heads (+8-24% vs +4-19%) and none in the monoarticular short head (+10% vs +9%) [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl]. Squats at either depth did not grow the hamstrings [@Kubo2019_squatDepth]. Supersets matched traditional sets for reps and volume load in less time, at a higher perceived effort [@Zhang2025_superset_meta].

exercises.name: Lying leg curl
exercises.summary: Knee flexion lying face down on a machine. It has no fixed slot: it replaces the [[ex:seated-leg-curl]] with the same sets and reps when your gym has no seated machine or it is taken ([[rule:substitution]]).
setup: Lie face down with your knees just off the end of the bench and the knee joint level with the machine's pivot.
Set the ankle pad on the back of your lower calves, just above the heels; hold the handles and press your hips into the bench.
execution: Start with the knees almost straight.
Curl the pad towards your backside in 1-2 s as far as you can without your hips lifting, and pause 1 s.
Lower over 2-3 s back to almost straight knees, keeping the stack off its rest.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you curl and in as you lower.
cues: Pull the pad up towards your backside.
Keep your hips pressed into the bench.
Lower the pad more slowly than you lifted it.

errors.error: Hips rise off the bench to finish the curl.
errors.fix: Use a lighter load, keep the hips pressed down and accept a slightly shorter curl.

errors.error: Swinging the weight up with momentum.
errors.fix: Pause 1 s at the top and lower over 2-3 s.

errors.error: Stopping short of straight at the bottom.
errors.fix: Let the knees almost straighten on every rep.

exercises.startingLoad: Light (for example 10-20 kg on the stack) for 12 reps at 3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]], then progress as for the seated curl.
exercises.effort: As for the seated curl: in [[phase:p1]] 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2, then 1-2 RIR; 0-2 RIR from [[phase:p2]]; failure on the last set is safe on this machine.
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]]: when all sets reach the top of the range, add one plate.
exercises.regression: A lighter load or a slower lowering.

alternatives.why: The preferred version: more hamstring growth because the hip is flexed.
Hamstrings at long length through a hip hinge.

exercises.whyChosen: It still grows the hamstrings well, just less than the seated version (see evidence). If the bench is angled at the hips, or you place a folded pad under your hips, the hip flexes slightly and the hamstrings work at a longer length (inference).
exercises.safety: Cramps in the hamstrings or calves near full contraction are common; stop and straighten the knee gently. Sharp pain at the back of the thigh: stop and follow [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: Lying flat keeps the hip nearly straight, so the biarticular hamstrings work at shorter lengths than when seated; the short head of biceps femoris, which crosses only the knee, is unaffected by hip position.
exercises.evidence: Lying curls increased whole-hamstring volume by 9% vs 14% for seated curls over 12 weeks; the monoarticular short head grew similarly with both (+9% vs +10%), and both protected similarly against later eccentric muscle damage [@Maeo2021_seatedVsProneCurl].

exercises.name: Leg extension (reclined)
exercises.summary: Seated knee extension on a machine, and the quadriceps [[term:isolation-exercise|isolation exercise]] on Lower A from [[phase:p2]] to [[phase:p4]] (12-15 reps, superset C). Recline the backrest if the machine allows: the reclined position grew rectus femoris, the quadriceps head that squats barely touch, more than sitting upright.
setup: Recline the backrest as far as it goes (the trial used a hip angle of about 40 degrees, torso well back). If it does not recline, sit upright; vastus lateralis, the only other head measured, grew equally in both positions.
Line your knee joint up with the machine's pivot, set the shin pad just above your ankles, and hold the handles to keep your hips on the seat.
execution: Start with the knees bent as far as the machine allows.
Extend in 1-2 s to almost straight and hold 1 s.
Lower over 2-3 s all the way back to the deepest bend, controlling this bottom part, where the quadriceps are longest.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you extend and in as you lower; keep breathing through the hard final reps.
cues: Kick the pad up towards the ceiling.
Let the pad sink all the way back under the seat.
Pull the handles to keep your seat glued down.

errors.error: Cutting the bottom of the range short.
errors.fix: Lower until the stack nearly touches down, reducing the load if needed.

errors.error: Kicking the weight up with momentum.
errors.fix: Pause 1 s at the top and lower over 2-3 s.

errors.error: Hips lift off the seat.
errors.fix: Pull on the handles and use a lighter load.

exercises.startingLoad: A light stack (for example 15-25 kg) for 15 reps, then add one plate per set until 12-15 reps leave 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]].
exercises.effort: 0-2 RIR. Failure is safe here, and with lighter loads getting close to failure matters a lot (see evidence). Optional on the last set: after the final full rep, add 4-6 partial reps in the bottom half ([[term:lengthened-partials|lengthened partials]]).
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]] within 12-15 reps: when all sets reach 15, add one plate.
exercises.regression: A lighter load, the upright position, or a pain-free shorter range if your knee is irritable ([[rule:pain]]).

alternatives.why: Compound quadriceps work, though it probably trains rectus femoris little (inference from squat data).
Quadriceps-heavy machine squat.

exercises.whyChosen: Squats did not grow rectus femoris, so a knee extension with the hip extended (reclined) fills the gap, and varied exercises grew all four quadriceps heads where a single exercise did not (see evidence). It sits in [[term:superset|superset]] C with the calf raise to save time.
exercises.safety: Knee extension loads the patellar tendon. Mild discomfort at the front of the knee that settles by the next day can be managed with the [[term:pain-monitoring|pain-monitoring model]]; sharp or worsening pain means stop and follow [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: Rectus femoris crosses the hip (as a hip flexor) and the knee. Reclining extends the hip, lengthening rectus femoris so it works over longer lengths, whereas in a squat the hip flexes as the knee flexes and its length barely changes. The three vasti cross only the knee; vastus lateralis, the one measured, grew equally in both positions.
exercises.evidence: Reclined (hip about 40 degrees) leg extensions grew rectus femoris more than upright ones (Bayes factor >100), with no difference for vastus lateralis [@Larsen2025_legExtHipAngle]. Squats grew neither rectus femoris nor the hamstrings [@Kubo2019_squatDepth], and only varied-exercise groups grew all four quadriceps heads significantly [@Fonseca2014_exerciseVariation]. With light loads, stopping short of failure gave far less growth (+2.8% vs +7.8%), but with heavy loads it barely mattered (+7.7% vs +8.1%) [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load]. Lengthened partials grew the quadriceps more than full range in untrained women [@Pedrosa2022_kneeExtLP], but a larger multi-site trial found the two practically equivalent for the thigh [@Gschneidner2025_lpROMmultisite], so full range stays the default.

exercises.name: Standing calf raise
equipment: standing calf machine, Smith machine or step
exercises.summary: Rising onto the balls of your feet with straight knees under load. It is the main calf exercise from week 3 of [[phase:p1]] (Full body B, superset E) and on Lower A from [[phase:p2]] to [[phase:p4]] (superset C). Knees straight, a full stretch at the bottom and a 1-2 s pause there on every rep.
setup: Standing calf machine: set the shoulder pads so you stand fully upright under load, balls of the feet on the edge of the block, heels free.
No machine: use a Smith machine with a step or plate under the balls of the feet, or stand on one leg on a step holding a dumbbell (left leg first).
execution: Lower your heels as far as they go over about 2 s and hold the deepest stretch for 1-2 s, without bouncing.
Rise in about 1 s as high as you can, pressing through the big-toe side of the foot, and hold 1 s.
Keep the knees straight but not forced back throughout.
exercises.breathing: Breathe steadily, out as you rise.
cues: Push the platform away through your big toes.
Drop your heels towards the floor and wait there.
Lift the shoulder pads as high as they will go.

errors.error: Bouncing out of the bottom.
errors.fix: Pause 1-2 s in the stretch so tendon recoil does not do the work.

errors.error: Bending the knees to help.
errors.fix: Use a lighter load and keep the knees straight so the gastrocnemius stays involved.

errors.error: Working only the top half of the range.
errors.fix: Lower fully every rep; the stretched half matters most.

exercises.startingLoad: Pick a load you can lift 15 times with 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] through the full range; once the pause is enforced it is often lighter than people expect (practical convention). For the single-leg step version, start at bodyweight.
exercises.effort: 0-2 RIR; the machine is safe to take to failure. Optional on the last set: after the final full rep, add 5-10 partial reps in the bottom (stretched) half.
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]] within the prescribed range (10-15, then 8-12 from [[phase:p3]]): when all sets reach the top with full pauses, add the smallest load step.
exercises.regression: Two-leg raises on a step at bodyweight, holding a support.

alternatives.why: Straight-knee calf work on the leg press when the calf machine is busy.
Trains springy, reactive calf and Achilles function for running and jumping, not size.

exercises.whyChosen: Standing (straight-knee) raises grew the gastrocnemius several times more than seated raises, and training the stretched part of the range added growth (see evidence). Calves show below shorts, so they matter for the look you are after.
exercises.safety: Build up the depth of the stretch over the first sessions, since the Achilles tendon adapts more slowly than muscle (practical convention). Mild Achilles discomfort that settles by the next morning can be managed with the [[term:pain-monitoring|pain-monitoring model]]: in one small trial in Achilles tendinopathy, continuing activity within pain-monitored limits improved as much as 6 weeks of active rest [@Silbernagel2007_painMonitoringRCT]. Anything sharper: [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: The gastrocnemius crosses both the knee and the ankle. With the knee straight it is lengthened and contributes fully; with the knee bent (seated) it is slack and the soleus does most of the work. The bottom, dorsiflexed position stretches it under load.
exercises.evidence: Compared with seated raises, standing raises grew lateral gastrocnemius +12.4% vs +1.7% and medial gastrocnemius +9.2% vs +0.6%, while the soleus grew similarly (+2.1% vs +2.9%) [@Kinoshita2023_standingVsSeatedCalf]. In untrained women, partial reps in the stretched half grew medial gastrocnemius more than full range (+15.2% vs +6.7%) [@Kassiano2023_calfLP], and adding stretched-position partials after failure added growth (+9.6% vs +6.7%) [@Larsen2025_calfPastFailure].

exercises.name: Calf press on the leg press
exercises.summary: Calf raises on the leg press: balls of the feet on the bottom edge of the platform, knees straight, you push the platform away using only your ankles. It is the Lower B calf exercise from [[phase:p2]] to [[phase:p4]] (12-20 reps, superset D), the straight-knee partner to the [[ex:standing-calf-raise]] on Lower A.
setup: Sit in the leg press as usual and push the sled up. Keep the safety stops engaged, or set them as high as they go, so the sled can only travel a few centimetres if your feet slip.
Place the balls of your feet on the bottom edge of the platform, hip-width, heels hanging off; knees straight but not locked hard.
execution: Let the platform push your toes back towards your shins over about 2 s, and hold the deepest stretch for 1-2 s.
Push through the balls of your feet to point your toes as far as you can in about 1 s, and hold 1 s.
Move only at the ankles; the knees stay straight throughout.
exercises.breathing: Breathe steadily, out as you push.
cues: Push the platform away with your big toes.
Let the platform push your toes towards your shins, and wait there.
Keep the sled moving only from your ankles.

errors.error: Feet slide on the platform.
errors.fix: Wear shoes with grip, put more of the forefoot on the plate and reduce the load.

errors.error: Knees bend to help.
errors.fix: Use a lighter load and keep the knees straight so the gastrocnemius works.

errors.error: Short, bouncing reps.
errors.fix: Take a full stretch with a pause on every rep.

exercises.startingLoad: Start at or below your leg-press warm-up load (for example the sled plus 20-40 kg) for 20 reps, adding 10 kg per set until 12-20 reps leave 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]].
exercises.effort: 0-2 RIR; calves tolerate sets close to failure well (practical convention). Stretched-position partials after the last full rep are optional, as on the standing raise.
exercises.progression: [[rule:double-progression]] within 12-20 reps: when all sets reach 20 with full pauses, add 10 kg.
exercises.regression: A lighter load, or the [[ex:standing-calf-raise]] at bodyweight on a step.

alternatives.why: The main straight-knee calf exercise on Lower A.
Reactive calf and Achilles work for running and jumping, not size.

exercises.whyChosen: It adds a second straight-knee calf exercise on a machine that is already set up for Lower B, and its 12-20 range spreads calf loading across rep ranges, which grow muscle similarly when sets are hard (see evidence). [[term:superset|Superset]] D keeps the session short.
exercises.safety: The main hazard is a foot slipping off the platform with straight knees, so keep the stops engaged, wear grippy shoes and stay at moderate loads until your foot position feels secure.
exercises.mechanism: As in the standing raise, the straight knee keeps the gastrocnemius lengthened so it shares the work with the soleus, and the dorsiflexed bottom position loads it while stretched.
exercises.evidence: Straight-knee raises grew the gastrocnemius far more than bent-knee raises (+9.2-12.4% vs +0.6-1.7%) [@Kinoshita2023_standingVsSeatedCalf]. Low, moderate and high loads produced similar hypertrophy [@Lopez2021_load_NMA], provided sets end close to failure [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load]. Supersets matched traditional sets for volume in less time [@Zhang2025_superset_meta], and in a 10-week trial leg-press gains were similar with supersets [@Iversen2024_superset_RCT].

exercises.name: Kettlebell swing
exercises.summary: A fast hip hinge: you hike a kettlebell back between your legs and snap your hips forward so it floats up to chest height. It is an option for the power and athletic work in [[phase:p3]] ([[dec:D17]]), training fast hip extension and, in longer sets, conditioning. It is a hip snap, not a squat, and your arms are only ropes.
setup: Place the bell about 30 cm in front of you, feet slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Hinge as in the RDL, grip the handle with both hands and tilt the bell towards you. Check the space in front of and behind you is clear.
execution: Hike the bell back high between your thighs, close to the groin, keeping the shins nearly vertical.
Snap the hips forward to stand tall; the bell floats forward and up to chest height on straight arms.
Let the bell fall and hinge back only as it reaches your hips, receiving it into the next backswing. Do sets of 10-15; to stop, let it swing back once and set it down in front of you.
exercises.breathing: A short, sharp exhale at the top of each swing; inhale as the bell drops into the backswing.
cues: Hike the bell back like a football snap.
Throw the bell forward with your hips.
Let the bell float to chest height.

errors.error: Squatting the swing: the knees bend a lot and the hips drop.
errors.fix: Hips back, shins nearly vertical; it is an RDL done fast.

errors.error: Lifting the bell with the arms or above the shoulders.
errors.fix: Keep the arms relaxed like ropes; the bell stops at chest height.

errors.error: Leaning back at the top.
errors.fix: Finish standing tall like a plank, ribs down.

errors.error: A low backswing, with the bell passing near the knees.
errors.fix: Hike it high, close to the groin.

exercises.startingLoad: A 12-16 kg kettlebell suits most beginners (practical convention). If your gym has few kettlebells, a dumbbell held vertically by one end can stand in.
exercises.effort: End each set while every swing is still crisp, far from failure, because speed is the point (practical convention for power work). Use 3-5 sets of 10-15.
exercises.progression: First a heavier bell, then more sets, rather than longer sets in which the reps slow down.
exercises.regression: Kettlebell Romanian deadlifts, or the [[ex:back-extension]].

alternatives.why: Slow hip-extension strength without the ballistic demand.
Fast hip extension through a jump instead of an implement.
The slow version of the same hinge.

exercises.whyChosen: Fast hip extension underpins jumping, sprinting and martial arts, and the swing trains it with minimal equipment once your RDLs have taught the hinge. Longer sets also add a short conditioning effect (inference).
exercises.safety: Check the space behind and in front of you before each set, keep your hands dry and never let go of the bell; if your grip fails, let it swing back down between your legs and set it down. Dropped weights caused two-thirds of weight-training injuries seen in emergency departments [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. Back pain during swings: switch to slow hinges and follow [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: The backswing loads the glutes and hamstrings [[term:eccentric|eccentrically]] and the hip snap is a rapid [[term:concentric|concentric]] hip extension; momentum then carries the bell, so the force is high and brief, much as in a jump (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: No catalogued trial tested the kettlebell swing, so its use here is practical convention. In dose-response modelling, power outcomes were best served by moderate loads (40-70% 1RM), unlike maximal strength, which favoured the heaviest loads [@Swinton2024_dose_response].

exercises.name: Trap-bar deadlift
exercises.summary: A deadlift from the floor using a hexagonal bar you stand inside, holding neutral-grip handles at your sides. It is the main lift on Lower B in weeks 9-16 of [[phase:p3]] (the strength block; reps set by the block, 180 s rest). The load sits in line with your body, so it is easier to learn than a straight-bar deadlift and shares the work between hips and knees.
setup: Stand in the centre of the bar, feet hip-width, with the handles level with the middle of your feet.
Hinge and bend your knees to grip the middle of the handles; use the raised handles if your bar has them, which suits tight hamstrings.
Arms straight, chest up, back neutral; pull the slack out until the bar is just about to leave the floor, then brace.
execution: Push the floor away so hips and shoulders rise together and the bar travels straight up; stand tall in 1-2 s.
Lower by pushing the hips back and bending the knees over about 2 s, and set the plates on the floor.
Reset every rep: let the plates settle, re-brace, then pull. No bouncing.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in and brace before each rep from the floor, hold it until you are standing, then breathe out at the top or once the bar is down.
cues: Push the floor away.
Keep the handles hanging straight below your shoulders.
Stand up tall between the handles.

errors.error: Hips shoot up first and the lift turns into a stiff-legged pull.
errors.fix: Start with the hips slightly lower and the chest up, and think 'push the floor away'.

errors.error: The back rounds as the bar leaves the floor.
errors.fix: Use the raised handles or stand the bar on 5-10 cm plates or mats, and take 10% off.

errors.error: Bouncing the plates between reps.
errors.fix: Let the bar settle completely and re-brace each rep.

exercises.startingLoad: Hex bars weigh about 20-30 kg, so check and note yours. Start with the bar plus 20 kg for 5-8 reps, then add 10-20 kg per [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up set]] until the block's reps leave 3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]].
exercises.effort: 2-3 RIR on every set, as the plan specifies; stop when a rep slows sharply or your back position changes. Never test a maximum alone ([[dec:D07]], [[dec:D16]]).
exercises.progression: When every set reaches the block's reps at 2-3 RIR, add 2.5-5 kg ([[rule:double-progression]]) and track strength with [[tool:e1rm]].
exercises.regression: Raise the bar on plates or blocks, or use the [[ex:bb-rdl]] from the rack or the [[ex:leg-press]].

alternatives.why: Hinge from the rack with no floor pull.
Heavy leg work with no load on the back.
The other heavy lower-body strength lift.

exercises.whyChosen: For a strength block it offers a heavy, simple lift that cannot trap you, because a failed rep just goes back to the floor. Strength is specific to the trained lift (see evidence), so a block of heavy pulling builds pulling strength directly.
exercises.safety: A trap bar can be set down or dropped safely, but keep your feet clear and the floor around you empty; dropped weights caused two-thirds of weight-training injuries seen in emergency departments [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. At 13:00, an hour after waking, ramp up gradually; the morning-disc caution in [[ex:db-rdl]] applies here too, more so from the floor (practical convention).
exercises.mechanism: Standing inside the bar puts the load's centre of mass in line with your feet and hips, shortening the lever arm at the hips and lower back compared with a straight bar in front of the shins. You can therefore start with more knee bend, so the quadriceps share the work (biomechanical reasoning, not tested in the catalogued trials).
exercises.evidence: Dynamic training improved strength in the trained task about twice as much as untrained isometric strength (SMD 0.98 vs 0.42) [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta]. Loads above 80% 1RM maximised strength, while hypertrophy was similar across prescriptions [@Currier2023_BJSM_NMA]. In 10 trained men, sets to failure slowed neuromuscular recovery by roughly 24-48 h compared with equal-volume non-failure sets [@MoranNavarro2017_failure_recovery], which supports stopping at 2-3 RIR (inference). Rests longer than 2 min appear needed to maximise strength once trained [@Grgic2018_rest_strength].

exercises.name: Incline dumbbell press (30 deg)
exercises.summary: Your main upper-chest press. It targets the clavicular head of the pectoralis major, the fibres under the collarbones that shape the top of the chest. It runs from Technique session B in [[phase:p0]] to the main press of Upper A in [[phase:p2]]-[[phase:p4]] (except weeks 1-16 of [[phase:p3]]; 150 s rest). Dumbbells suit training alone: a failed rep can be dropped to the sides.
setup: Set the backrest to the notch nearest 30° (45° if that is the closest); note the notch in Hevy and reuse it every week.
Take the dumbbells from the rack, sit with them on your thighs, lie back and bump them up to your chest with your knees.
Feet flat, shoulder blades pulled back and down into the pad, a small natural arch in your lower back.
execution: Press up and slightly in until your arms are straight over your upper chest (about 1 s); the dumbbells need not touch.
Lower for 2-3 s with your elbows 45-60° from your sides and forearms vertical.
Stop when the dumbbells are level with your chest and you feel a firm stretch; pause briefly, no bounce. Use this full [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] on every rep.
To finish, lower the dumbbells to your chest, then sit up with them resting on your thighs.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in on the way down and out as you press.
