On the last hard reps a short held breath through the sticking point is fine (a brief [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]]); do not hold it across several grinding reps, when blood-pressure peaks are highest [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting].
cues: Drive the dumbbells to the ceiling above your collarbones.
Trace an upside-down V: wide at the bottom, close at the top.
Keep your upper back glued to the pad.
Push the floor away with your feet.

errors.error: Stopping well above the chest to use heavier dumbbells.
errors.fix: Take a lighter pair and lower until the dumbbells are level with your chest.

errors.error: Elbows flared out to 90°.
errors.fix: Tuck them to 45-60° so the dumbbells come down beside your upper chest.

errors.error: Lifting dumbbells off the floor with straight legs.
errors.fix: With your tight hamstrings that reach loads your lower back; take them from the rack or squat down with bent knees.

exercises.startingLoad: In [[phase:p0]] use a pair you could press about 14 times but stop at 10, which is about 4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. From a 5-push-up baseline that is likely 5-10 kg per dumbbell (inference; your [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] decide). Ramp up with about 8 easy reps at half that weight and 3-4 at three-quarters ([[tool:warmup]]). Log the weight of one dumbbell.
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 2-3 RIR (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 7-8; RPE is about 10 minus RIR); about 4 RIR in [[phase:p0]] and 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2 of [[phase:p1]]. Never grind a rep you might fail over your face ([[dec:D07]]); check your estimates with [[rule:rir-calibration]].
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]): when every set reaches the top of the rep range at the target RIR, take the next pair and restart near the bottom of the range. Gym dumbbells usually rise in 2-2.5 kg steps; if the jump is too big, add reps on the lighter pair until the heavier one allows the bottom of the range. Stalled: [[rule:stall]].
exercises.regression: Lower the bench one notch, or use [[ex:machine-chest-press]] while the dumbbells feel unsteady. For shoulder discomfort, shorten the bottom of the range slightly and follow [[rule:pain]].

alternatives.why: Same angle on a fixed path; easier to load heavily alone once getting dumbbells into position becomes the limit.
The most stable press and safe near failure alone, with less upper-chest bias.
When no adjustable bench is free; shifts work toward the middle and lower chest.

exercises.whyChosen: Incline pressing is the only press with a trial showing extra upper-chest growth ([[dec:D08]], [[dec:D12]]). Free weights and machines grow muscle similarly on average [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], so safety and range decided the tool: dumbbells cannot pin you, and they travel deeper than a bar that stops on your chest (practical convention).
exercises.safety:
!> If a rep stalls, lower the dumbbells to your chest and let them roll off to the sides; rehearse this once with a light pair. About two-thirds of weight-training injuries seen in US emergency departments came from a weight dropping on the lifter [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED].

You lift about an hour after waking, so do the general warm-up ([[ex:wu-band-dislocate]], [[ex:wu-scap-pushup]]) before your ramp-up sets (practical convention). Sharp or catching pain in the shoulder ends the set ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: The clavicular fibres run up and out toward the collarbone, so pressing over the upper chest with some shoulder flexion lines them up with the load (anatomical reasoning). Incline pressing raised clavicular-head electrical activity (EMG) and acute swelling, while flat pressing favoured the sternocostal head [@Albarello2022_pecInclineAcute], and in one small uncontrolled triceps study regional growth tracked regional activation [@Wakahara2013_nonuniform].
exercises.evidence: In untrained young men, 8 weeks of once-weekly incline pressing grew the upper pectoral site more than flat pressing (mean difference 0.62 cm, [[term:confidence-interval|95% confidence interval]] 0.23-1.0), with similar strength gains; only one of three sites differed [@Chaves2020_inclineVsFlat]. It is one low-certainty trial, so trust the direction more than the size; the best angle is untested. Resting longer than about 90 s adds little for growth [@Singer2024_rest_meta]; the 150 s in later phases is there for heavier sets (inference).

exercises.name: Flat dumbbell bench press
exercises.summary: The flat dumbbell press trains the whole chest, with more work for the middle and lower fibres than the incline version. You learn it in Technique session A ([[phase:p0]]); it is the primary press of Full body B in [[phase:p1]] (8-12 reps, 90 s rest) and later the second press on Upper B days.
setup: Take the dumbbells from the rack, sit on the end of a flat bench with them on your thighs, lie back and bump them to your chest with your knees.
Feet flat and a little wider than the bench, shoulder blades pulled back and down, a small natural arch.
Start with the dumbbells over your lower chest, palms toward your feet or angled slightly in.
execution: Lower for 2-3 s with elbows 45-60° from your sides until the dumbbells are level with your chest and you feel a firm stretch.
Pause briefly without bouncing, then press up and slightly in over your lower chest (about 1 s).
Stop at straight arms without letting your shoulders lift off the pad; full [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] every rep.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in on the way down and out as you press. A short held breath through the sticking point on the last hard reps is acceptable (a brief [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]]); never hold it across several grinding reps [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting].
cues: Push the dumbbells up toward the ceiling over your lower chest.
Lower the handles until they line up with your chest.
Keep your upper back pressed into the pad.
Push the floor away with your feet.

errors.error: Shoulders rolling forward off the pad at the top.
errors.fix: Finish at straight arms with your shoulder blades still pulled back.

errors.error: Elbows flared to 90° with the dumbbells drifting toward your neck.
errors.fix: Tuck the elbows to 45-60° so the dumbbells stay over your lower chest.

errors.error: Half reps that stop well above the chest.
errors.fix: Use a lighter pair and lower until the dumbbells are level with your chest.

exercises.startingLoad: In [[phase:p0]] use a pair you could press about 14 times but stop at 10, about 4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; expect it to be slightly heavier than your incline pair (inference). Do 1-2 [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] first ([[tool:warmup]]); when it is the first press of a session an hour after waking, keep the second one (practical convention). Log the weight of one dumbbell.
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 2-3 RIR (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 7-8); about 4 RIR in [[phase:p0]] and 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2 of [[phase:p1]]; no failed reps with dumbbells over your face ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]): when every set reaches the top of the range at the target RIR, take the next pair and restart near the bottom. If the 2-2.5 kg step is too big, add reps on the lighter pair first. Stalled: [[rule:stall]].
exercises.regression: Use [[ex:machine-chest-press]], or [[ex:push-up]] with your hands raised on a bench, while the dumbbells feel unsteady. For shoulder discomfort, shorten the bottom slightly and follow [[rule:pain]].

alternatives.why: Same pattern without the balance demand; safe near failure alone.
Heavier loading for strength, used only in [[phase:p3]] inside a rack with [[term:safety-arms|safety arms]].
No equipment; the same pattern at bodyweight when benches are taken.

exercises.whyChosen: The flat press loads the middle and lower chest, complementing the incline press ([[dec:D08]]). Dumbbells were preferred to a barbell for a solo novice because they can be dumped safely, each arm finds a comfortable path and they allow a deeper stretch (practical convention). In a matched trial in trained men, pectoral growth differed by 2% or less between free-weight and machine training [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT].
exercises.safety:
!> If a rep stalls, lower the dumbbells to your chest and let them roll off to the sides; never drop them from straight arms.

Free weights were involved in 90% of weight-training injuries seen in US emergency departments, mostly through dropped weights [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. Sharp or catching shoulder pain ends the set ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: Flat pressing is mainly horizontal adduction of the upper arm, along the line of the sternocostal fibres, which acute data show it favours [@Albarello2022_pecInclineAcute]. Dumbbells can travel below the line of the chest, loading the pectorals at a longer length; a review argues that loading a muscle hard at long lengths tends to produce more growth [@Pedrosa2026_muscleLengthReview], though measured regional differences are small.
exercises.evidence: Pooled trials found no difference in muscle growth between free weights and machines ([[term:smd|standardised mean difference (SMD)]] -0.055, with a wide interval) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta]. Full range of motion gave larger strength gains than partial range (effect size 0.56) [@Pallares2021_ROMmeta]. Lowering speed matters little: growth was similar across repetition durations of 0.5-8 s [@Schoenfeld2015_rep_duration], so the 2-3 s lowering is for control (practical convention).

exercises.name: Machine chest press
exercises.summary: A seated, guided chest press: the most stable press in the programme and the one you can push closest to failure alone, because letting go simply returns the stack. It is the second press on Upper B in [[phase:p3]] (8-12 reps, 90 s rest) and a stand-in for any chest press when benches are busy.
setup: Set the seat so the handles line up with your mid-chest; note the seat number in Hevy.
Back and head on the pad, feet flat, shoulder blades pulled back and down.
Grip with straight wrists and your elbows 45-60° from your sides.
execution: Press until your arms are straight but not jammed (about 1 s).
Return for 2-3 s until the handles are just in front of your chest and you feel a stretch.
Reverse just before the plates touch; full [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] every rep.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you press and in as the handles return. On a machine you can keep breathing on every rep even in hard sets, so do.
cues: Push the handles toward the far wall.
Keep your back and head on the pad.
Let the stack hover, never rest, between reps.

errors.error: Seat too low, so the handles sit at your shoulders.
errors.fix: Raise the seat until the handles meet your mid-chest.

errors.error: Shoulders shrugging forward off the pad at lockout.
errors.fix: Stop at straight arms with your back still on the pad.

errors.error: Resting the stack between reps.
errors.fix: Reverse just before the plates touch.

exercises.startingLoad: Choose a pin you could press about 15 times and do 10-12 in the first session. Stacks may be marked in kg, lb or plain numbers, so log exactly what the stack shows plus the machine name; machine numbers do not translate to dumbbell weights (practical convention).
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-9), and the last set may reach [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] ([[dec:D07]]). Such a set is also the safest way to check your RIR estimates ([[rule:rir-calibration]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]): when every set reaches 12 at the target RIR, move the pin one step and restart at 8. If a step is too big, use the machine's small add-on weight if it has one.
exercises.regression: Use a lighter pin and a slightly shorter stretch if the shoulder complains ([[rule:pain]]); this is already the easiest press to learn.

alternatives.why: Free-weight version of the same pattern, with a deeper stretch.
Shifts the work toward the upper chest.
When every machine is taken.

exercises.whyChosen: Machines were put first for a solo novice ([[dec:D08]]): nothing to balance, no spotter needed, and growth similar to free weights on average [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta]. That makes this the safest place to train hard.
exercises.safety: Keep your fingers clear of the stack and moving levers. In emergency-department data, machine injuries were less often fractures or dislocations than free-weight injuries (9.7% vs 23.6%) [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED].
exercises.mechanism: The fixed path removes most of the stabilising work, so more of each set's effort reaches the pectorals, deltoids and triceps (inference). In 10 trained men, sets taken to failure depleted type II fibre glycogen (an indirect index of recruitment) similarly with heavy and light loads [@Morton2019_fibre_activation], which suggests effort matters more than the exact pin (inference).
exercises.evidence: In a matched 8-week trial in trained men, pectoralis major cross-sectional area rose with both free weights and machines, with differences of 2% or less [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT]. Going all the way to failure added little over stopping just short (effect size 0.12, not significant) [@Refalo2023_failure_hypertrophy], and RIR guesses are most accurate close to failure [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy].

exercises.name: Incline press (Smith machine)
exercises.summary: The incline press on a bar that runs in fixed rails. It is the main press of Upper A in the first 8 weeks of [[phase:p3]] (150 s rest), when dumbbells heavy enough for you become awkward to get into position alone. Set safety stops make heavy sets safe without a spotter.
setup: Put an adjustable bench in the Smith machine at the notch nearest 30°, placed so the bar meets your upper chest just below the collarbones.
Set the safety stops just below the bar's lowest point on your chest and test them with the empty bar.
Grip slightly wider than shoulder width, shoulder blades back and down, feet flat. Note the bench position in Hevy.
execution: Rotate the bar off the hooks and lower it for 2-3 s to touch your upper chest lightly, elbows 45-60° from your sides.
Press to straight arms (about 1 s) without lifting your shoulders off the pad; full [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] every rep.
Rack by rotating the hooks onto the pegs at the top of a rep.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in on the way down and out as you press. On heavy sets a short held breath from the bottom through the sticking point (a brief [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]]) is acceptable, never across grinding reps [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting].
cues: Drive the bar straight up the rails.
Touch the same spot below your collarbones every rep.
Push the floor away with your feet.

errors.error: Bench in the wrong place, so the bar lands on your neck or mid-chest.
errors.fix: Move it with the empty bar until the bar meets your upper chest.

errors.error: Safety stops too low to catch the bar.
errors.fix: Set them so the bar rests on them just below your chest-touch point.

errors.error: Bouncing the bar off your chest.
errors.fix: Touch lightly, then press.

exercises.startingLoad: Smith bars differ in weight (some are counterbalanced), so find your load with [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]]: the empty bar for 10, then heavier steps until a load would leave about 2 reps spare at the target ([[tool:warmup]]). Log the plates plus one fixed bar figure for that machine.
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-9) in your phase's main rep range. The stops make a missed rep safe, but it still costs recovery, so plan not to miss ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: Follow the [[phase:p3]] block plan ([[dec:D16]]); within it, add the smallest plates available once every set reaches the top of the range ([[rule:double-progression]]).
exercises.regression: Return to [[ex:incline-db-press]] with lighter dumbbells, or use [[ex:machine-chest-press]] if the fixed path bothers your shoulders ([[rule:pain]]).

alternatives.why: Free-weight version; each arm finds its own path.
When the Smith machine is busy or the fixed path feels wrong.

exercises.whyChosen: It keeps the upper-chest bias of incline pressing [@Chaves2020_inclineVsFlat] and removes the two problems of heavy dumbbells alone: getting them into position and bailing out ([[dec:D15]]).
exercises.safety:
!> Set and test the safety stops every session before loading the bar, and check the hooks have engaged before letting go.

For a solo lifter the main acute risk is being trapped or struck by a weight; about two-thirds of emergency-department weight-training injuries came from a weight dropping on the lifter [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED].
exercises.mechanism: The rails take over balancing, so more effort goes into pushing, and the line of push over the upper chest favours the clavicular fibres as it does with dumbbells [@Albarello2022_pecInclineAcute]. Strength gained on a fixed path transfers only partly to free weights.
exercises.evidence: Free-weight and machine training gave similar growth, but strength was modality-specific: free-weight-tested strength improved more with free weights ([[term:smd|standardised mean difference (SMD)]] -0.21) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta]. Expect your dumbbell press to feel slightly rusty when it returns in week 17, and judge progress within each exercise (inference).

exercises.name: Barbell bench press
equipment: bench in rack with safety arms
exercises.summary: The classic heavy press, used only in the [[phase:p3]] strength block (weeks 9-16, Upper A, 180 s rest) and only inside a rack with [[term:safety-arms|safety arms]]. It allows the heaviest pressing loads in the programme, which is what builds maximal strength.
setup: In a power rack, set the bench so your eyes are under the bar, and set the safety arms about 2 cm below the bar's height when it touches your chest with your normal arch.
Test with the empty bar: lower it to your chest, flatten your back, and it should settle on the arms.
Grip slightly wider than shoulder width, shoulder blades back and down, feet flat; use collars.
execution: Unrack to straight arms over your shoulders, then bring the bar over your lower chest.
Lower for about 2 s to touch your lower chest, elbows 45-70° from your sides, forearms vertical.
Press up and slightly back toward your shoulders as fast as the load allows; full [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] every rep.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in at the top, hold it while you lower and press ([[term:bracing|bracing]] with a brief [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]]), and breathe out at the top. Release it within each rep, never across a slow grind [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting].
cues: Push yourself away from the bar into the bench.
Drive the bar up and back toward the rack uprights.
Try to bend the bar in half with your grip.
Push the floor away with your feet.

errors.error: Safety arms too low to catch the bar.
errors.fix: Reset them about 2 cm below chest height and retest with the empty bar.

errors.error: Bouncing the bar off the chest.
errors.fix: Touch, then press.

errors.error: Hips lifting off the bench.
errors.fix: Keep your glutes on the pad and push through your feet without lifting.

exercises.startingLoad: Do not test a maximum. In week 9, ramp up from the empty bar (usually 20 kg) in 5-10 kg steps until a load leaves about 3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] at the target reps ([[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]], [[tool:warmup]]). Instead of a true [[term:1rm|one-repetition maximum (1RM)]], track an [[term:e1rm|estimated 1RM (e1RM)]] with [[tool:e1rm]].
exercises.effort: Never to failure: end every set at 2-3 RIR (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8 at most) ([[dec:D07]], [[dec:D15]]). In 10 trained men, failure on heavy bench and squat sets slowed recovery by about 24-48 h compared with equal-volume sets stopped short [@MoranNavarro2017_failure_recovery].
exercises.progression: Follow the block structure in [[dec:D16]]: when all sets reach the target reps at the target RIR, add 2.5 kg (1.25 kg per side), or less if the gym has fractional plates.
exercises.regression: Use [[ex:db-bench-press]] or [[ex:machine-chest-press]] if no rack with safety arms is free, or if the fixed hand position bothers your shoulders ([[rule:pain]]).

alternatives.why: Same pattern, safe to dump, lighter loads.
Heavy pressing with no free weight above you.

exercises.whyChosen: Strength is specific to what you train: free-weight-tested strength improved more with free weights [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], and heavier loads gave larger strength gains with similar growth [@Lopez2021_load_NMA]. A short barbell block is worth it once technique is stable and safety arms remove the solo risk ([[dec:D15]]).
exercises.safety:
!!> Never bench a barbell alone without safety arms. Many commercial gyms have fixed bench stations with uprights but no safeties (practical observation); if that is all yours has, use the Smith machine or dumbbells.

If a rep fails, lower the bar to your chest, flatten your back so it settles on the arms, and slide out toward your head. Weights dropping on the lifter caused 65.5% of emergency-department weight-training injuries [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. This is your heaviest lift of the day, an hour after waking, so do not skimp on the warm-up.
exercises.mechanism: Early strength gains are largely [[term:neural-adaptation|neural adaptation]]: better coordination and higher [[term:motor-unit|motor-unit]] firing rates in the trained movement [@Skarabot2021_neural_review]. Heavy loads practise exactly that (inference), which is why this block uses lower reps and longer rests.
exercises.evidence: Across trials, loads above 80% of 1RM maximised strength while growth was similar across prescriptions [@Currier2023_BJSM_NMA]; rests longer than 2 min appear needed to maximise strength in trained people [@Grgic2018_rest_strength]. Trained lifters judged bench-press RIR to within about 0.65 reps [@Refalo2024_RIRaccuracyBench]; after two phases of practice yours should be close (inference).

exercises.name: Push-up (with progressions)
exercises.summary: The bodyweight press and your muscular-endurance marker, retested in the [[ex:test-pushup]]. Your baseline is 5 floor reps, so you train it with your hands raised and work down toward the floor. It also stands in for a dumbbell press when benches are taken or you are away from the gym.
setup: Incline level: hands on a bench or, better, on a Smith-machine bar locked at a set height, which can be lowered one notch at a time; note the notch.
Hands slightly wider than your shoulders, body straight from head to heels, glutes and abdominals tight.
Floor level: the same position on the floor. Deficit level: hands on two dumbbells or plates.
execution: Lower for about 2 s as one unit, elbows 30-60° from your sides, until your chest almost touches the bar, bench or floor.
Push back to straight arms (about 1 s), letting your shoulder blades spread apart at the top.
Every rep reaches the same depth; when one cannot, the set is over.
exercises.breathing: In on the way down, out on the way up; breathe on every rep.
cues: Push the floor away.
Move like a plank: hips and shoulders arrive together.
Screw your hands into the floor.

errors.error: Hips sagging or piking up.
errors.fix: Squeeze your glutes; if the line still breaks, raise your hands higher.

errors.error: Shrinking the range as you tire.
errors.fix: End the set when depth goes, or raise the hands, rather than shortening reps.

errors.error: Elbows flared to 90°.
errors.fix: Keep them 30-60° from your sides.

exercises.startingLoad: Find the hand height where you can do 8-12 good reps with about 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; from a 5-rep floor baseline that is probably a bar or bench around hip height (inference). Your 60 s plank suggests the trunk will not be the limit.
exercises.effort: As training, end sets at 1-2 RIR (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-9); bodyweight sets are safe to take to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] now and then. In the test, go to failure with strict form.
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] by height: when every set reaches 15, lower the bar one notch and restart near 8. Order: incline, floor, deficit or feet on a bench, then weighted (a backpack with plates is easier alone than a plate on your back).
exercises.regression: Raise the hands higher; a wall is the easiest. Raised-hand push-ups keep the full-body line that kneeling versions lose (practical convention).

alternatives.why: Loadable in small steps once push-ups pass about 20 reps.
The same pattern with simple load control.

exercises.whyChosen: It needs no equipment, trains the serratus anterior and trunk along with the pressers, and gives a simple endurance measure you can retest anywhere. Light loads taken to failure grew muscle about as well as heavy ones [@Schoenfeld2017_load_meta], so high-rep push-up sets count as growth work when they end at or very near failure.
exercises.safety: Low risk. For wrist discomfort, hold dumbbell handles to keep your wrists straight. Sharp shoulder pain ends the set ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: Raising the hands shifts more of your weight onto your feet, so the arms push less (simple mechanics). Unlike on a bench, the shoulder blades move freely, so the serratus anterior works to spread them at the top.
exercises.evidence: Light (more than 15 reps possible), moderate and heavy loads produced similar [[term:hypertrophy|hypertrophy]] [@Lopez2021_load_NMA], but with light loads effort decides the result: in a knee-extension trial, sets at 30% of [[term:1rm|1RM]] grew the quadriceps by 7.8% when taken to failure and by only 2.8% when stopped short [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load].

exercises.name: Seated dumbbell shoulder press
exercises.summary: A seated overhead press with your back supported, for the front and side of the shoulders and the triceps. You learn it in Technique session B ([[phase:p0]], 75 s rest) and use it on Upper B in [[phase:p2]]-[[phase:p4]] (8-12 reps, 90 s rest). You can raise your arms overhead without arching your lower back, which makes the seated version a good fit.
setup: Set the backrest upright or one notch below, and the seat to its first notch so you do not slide.
Sit with the dumbbells on your thighs, then lift one knee at a time, left first, to bring each to your shoulder.
Back and head on the pad, feet flat and wide, dumbbells just outside your shoulders, palms forward or angled slightly in.
execution: Press up and slightly in until your arms are straight beside your ears (about 1 s); the dumbbells need not touch.
Lower for 2-3 s until the handles are at about chin to ear height, elbows slightly in front of your body.
Keep your lower back on the pad throughout; full [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] every rep.
exercises.breathing: In on the way down, out as you press. A short held breath through the sticking point on the hardest reps (a brief [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]]) is fine, never across grinding reps [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting].
cues: Drive the dumbbells to the ceiling.
Keep your lower back on the pad.
Bring the handles down to ear height every rep.

errors.error: Arching the lower back off the pad to finish reps.
errors.fix: Lighten the load; end the set when your back starts to peel off.

errors.error: Elbows flared straight out to the sides at the bottom.
errors.fix: Bring them about 30° in front of your body.

errors.error: Cutting the bottom short.
errors.fix: Lower to about chin height on every rep.

exercises.startingLoad: In [[phase:p0]] choose a pair you could press about 14 times and stop at 10, about 4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; likely 4-8 kg per dumbbell from your baseline (inference). One [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up set]] at half the weight is enough if you have already pressed that session.
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 2-3 RIR (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 7-8), about 4 RIR in [[phase:p0]]. Overhead dumbbells are awkward to bail from, so stop a rep early rather than grind ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]). A 2-2.5 kg step is a big relative jump at these weights, so expect to sit at the top of the range for a session or two before the heavier pair allows 8 reps.
exercises.regression: Use [[ex:machine-shoulder-press]], or shorten the bottom of the range slightly if the shoulder is uncomfortable ([[rule:pain]]).

alternatives.why: Same pattern, no balancing, safe near failure alone.
If overhead pressing irritates the shoulder; keeps the side deltoid trained, though it does not build pressing strength.

exercises.whyChosen: Overhead pressing adds deltoid and triceps work that chest presses do not fully cover. The seated, back-supported version removes trunk balance from the task, and dumbbells can be lowered to the thighs or set down beside you (practical convention). How much it adds to the side deltoid beyond raises is inference ([[dec:D12]]).
exercises.safety:
!> To bail, lower the dumbbells to your shoulders and then to your thighs, or set them down beside you; never let them fall forward or overhead.

In competitive weight-training sports the shoulder is among the most often injured sites, and strains and tendinitis are among the commonest injury types [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury]. Pain that is sharp, or grows from set to set, means stop ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: Pressing overhead combines shoulder flexion and abduction, driven by the anterior and lateral deltoids, while the triceps straighten the elbow and the trapezius and serratus anterior rotate the shoulder blade upward. Elbows slightly forward, in the plane of the shoulder blade, usually feels best for the joint (practical convention).
exercises.evidence: No longitudinal trial compares overhead pressing with lateral raises for side-deltoid growth, so using both rests on anatomical inference. Free weights and machines give similar growth [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], so swapping to the machine costs little. For untrained people, 60-120 s between sets appears sufficient for strength gains [@Grgic2018_rest_strength].

exercises.name: Machine shoulder press
exercises.summary: The guided overhead press: a fixed path, no balancing, and the load returns to the stack if you let go. Use it in place of [[ex:db-shoulder-press]] when dumbbells are busy, when getting them to your shoulders is awkward, or when you want to take sets close to failure safely.
setup: Set the seat so the handles start at or just above shoulder height; note the seat number in Hevy.
Back and head on the pad, feet flat, grip just outside shoulder width.
execution: Press until your arms are straight, without shrugging (about 1 s).
Lower for 2-3 s until the handles are at chin to ear height, reversing just before the stack touches.
Keep your lower back on the pad; full [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] every rep.
exercises.breathing: Out as you press, in as you lower; breathe on every rep.
cues: Push the handles to the ceiling.
Keep the stack hovering between reps.
Keep your back on the pad.

errors.error: Seat so high that the range is tiny.
errors.fix: Lower it until the handles start at shoulder height.

errors.error: Lower back arching off the pad.
errors.fix: Reduce the load and keep contact.

errors.error: Shrugging at the top.
errors.fix: Stop at straight arms with your shoulders down.

exercises.startingLoad: A pin you could press about 15 times, done for 10-12. Log the pin and machine name; plate-loaded and pin-loaded machines are not comparable (practical convention).
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-9); the last set may reach [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]): at the top of the range on every set, move one pin step and restart at the bottom.
exercises.regression: Shorten the bottom of the range slightly if the shoulder is uncomfortable ([[rule:pain]]).

alternatives.why: The free-weight default in the programme.
If pressing overhead hurts; keeps the side deltoid trained.

exercises.whyChosen: Same muscles and pattern as the dumbbell press with fewer things to control; machine and free-weight training grow muscle similarly [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta] ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: Keep your fingers clear of the levers and the stack. Machine injuries in emergency-department data were less often fractures or dislocations than free-weight injuries [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED].
exercises.mechanism: With the path fixed, stabilising muscles work less and the deltoids and triceps can be taken closer to failure safely; the strength you gain is partly specific to the machine [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta].
exercises.evidence: In a matched trial in trained men, strength and muscle-size changes differed by 2% or less between free-weight and machine training [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT]. Sets stopped just short of failure capture most of the benefit (failure vs non-failure effect size 0.12, not significant) [@Refalo2023_failure_hypertrophy].

exercises.name: Dumbbell lateral raise
exercises.summary: Your main [[term:isolation-exercise|isolation exercise]] for the side (lateral) deltoid, the muscle that widens the shoulders and makes the waist look narrower by contrast. Learned in [[phase:p0]], it is a priority exercise on Upper B in [[phase:p2]]-[[phase:p4]] (12-20 reps, 45 s rest, in a [[term:superset|superset]]). Loads are light; strict reps matter more than weight.
setup: Stand with feet hip-width and knees soft, and tip your torso about 10-15° forward from the hips; this small hinge does not need hamstring flexibility.
Hold the dumbbells beside your thighs, palms in, elbows slightly bent and fixed.
execution: Raise the dumbbells out to the sides, elbows leading, until your upper arms are about level with your shoulders (1-2 s).
Pause briefly at the top with your hands no higher than your elbows.
Lower for 2-3 s to just short of your thighs and start the next rep without resting at the bottom.
exercises.breathing: Out as you raise, in as you lower; the loads are light, so breathe continuously.
cues: Push the dumbbells out toward the side walls.
Lead with the elbows; let the dumbbells trail.
Keep the dumbbells level with the floor at the top.

errors.error: Swinging the torso to get the dumbbells up.
errors.fix: Use a lighter pair; only your arms move.

errors.error: Shrugging toward your ears.
errors.fix: Keep a long neck and stop the raise at shoulder height.

errors.error: Raising far above shoulder height.
errors.fix: Stop with the upper arm level; going higher mainly adds trapezius work (practical convention).

exercises.startingLoad: Start light: often 2-5 kg per dumbbell for a novice (inference). In [[phase:p0]] pick the pair you could raise about 16 times and do 12 clean reps.
exercises.effort: In [[phase:p0]] stop about 4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] short, and at 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2 of [[phase:p1]]; after that end sets at 0-2 RIR (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-10), since light dumbbells are safe near failure. RIR guesses are least accurate in sets above 12 reps [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy], so take a last set to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] now and then to recalibrate ([[rule:rir-calibration]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] across 12-20 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). Going from 5 to 7.5 kg is a 50% jump, so build to 20 reps before moving up and expect about 12 with the new pair; [[ex:cable-lateral-raise]] offers smaller steps.
exercises.regression: Do them seated, or lying chest-down on an incline bench, if you cannot stop swinging.

alternatives.why: Equal growth in a trial, with smoother loading at the bottom and finer weight steps.
Trains the deltoids if raises irritate the shoulder, though no trial shows it replaces raises for the side head.

exercises.whyChosen: Shoulder width matters for the look you want: in photo-rating studies, perceived strength explained over 70% of the variance in rated male bodily attractiveness among mostly Western student raters [@Sell2017_strengthAttractiveness], and a V-shaped torso was the main predictor for urban British and Malaysian women raters [@Swami2005_WCRcrossCultural]. Pressing does not single out the side deltoid, so a direct raise is added (anatomical inference; [[dec:D12]]).
exercises.safety: Low risk at these loads. For pinching at the top of the shoulder, stop just below shoulder height and lean a little further forward; persistent pain: [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: The lateral deltoid abducts the arm. A dumbbell's resistance peaks when the arm is horizontal and is near zero at the bottom, so the top half does most of the loading; a cable shifts some of it lower (mechanics).
exercises.evidence: Over 8 weeks in trained lifters, dumbbell and cable raises increased lateral deltoid thickness by 3.3-4.6%, with no difference between them [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable]. Light loads grew muscle about as well as heavy ones when sets went to failure [@Schoenfeld2017_load_meta], and supersets keep growth similar while saving time (standardised effect -0.05) [@Zhang2025_superset_meta].

exercises.name: Cable lateral raise
exercises.summary: A one-arm lateral raise from a low pulley, left arm first, and your most frequent side-deltoid exercise: Full body B in [[phase:p1]], then both Upper A and Lower B in [[phase:p2]]-[[phase:p4]] (12-20 reps per side, 45 s rest, in a [[term:superset|superset]]). The cable keeps tension at the bottom and allows finer weight steps than dumbbells.
setup: Set the pulley at its lowest point with a single D-handle, or hold the cable ball.
Stand side-on with the machine on your right, take the handle in your left hand in front of your body, and hold the frame with your right hand.

Step out until the stack lifts slightly at the start, and lean a little away from the machine. Midday is usually off-peak in commercial gyms, so a cable station is easier to hold for the superset (practical observation).
execution: Raise your left arm out to the side, elbow slightly bent and leading, until the upper arm is level with your shoulder (1-2 s).
Lower for 2-3 s until your hand is in front of your hip, keeping the cable taut.
Finish the left side, turn round and match its rep count on the right; rest once both sides are done.
exercises.breathing: Out as you raise, in as you lower; breathe continuously.
cues: Push the handle out toward the far wall.
Keep the stack moving smoothly, with no clank at the bottom.
Sweep the handle through a wide arc.

errors.error: Leaning further away each rep to heave the weight up.
errors.fix: Set your lean at the start; only the arm moves.

errors.error: Shrugging toward the ear.
errors.fix: Keep the shoulder down and stop at shoulder height.

errors.error: Letting the stack rest between reps.
errors.fix: Reverse just before the plates touch.

exercises.startingLoad: The lightest pin, or one step up, for 12-15 controlled reps. Pulley ratios differ between cable stations, so log the station in Hevy notes and compare only like with like (practical convention).
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-10), or 3-4 RIR in weeks 1-2 of [[phase:p1]]; the last set on each side may safely reach [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] over 12-20 reps per side ([[rule:double-progression]]). If a full pin step is too big, use the stack's add-on weight if it has one.
exercises.regression: Raise only to about two-thirds of shoulder height, or use [[ex:db-lateral-raise]] with light dumbbells.

alternatives.why: Equal growth in a trial; needs no free cable station.
If raises irritate the shoulder; not a like-for-like replacement for the side head.

exercises.whyChosen: It matches dumbbell raises for growth [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable] and adds variety for a muscle you train often. Working one arm at a time, left first and matching the reps on the right, carries over the left-first habit from your single-leg work ([[dec:D28]]) and keeps the two sides even (practical convention).
exercises.safety: Low risk. You step and turn between sides, so keep the floor around you clear. For pain at the top of the shoulder, lower the height and see [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: A low cable pulls down and across the body, so the deltoid is loaded even near the bottom, where a dumbbell's resistance is close to zero. Whether that extra low-range loading adds growth is untested for the deltoid, and the equal-growth trial suggests it matters little [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable].
exercises.evidence: [[term:unilateral|Unilateral]] and bilateral training produced similar muscle growth (effect size -0.21, very imprecise), with strength specific to the version trained [@Kassiano2025_uniVsBiMeta], so the one-arm format is for control and evenness rather than extra growth. Lateral deltoid thickness rose 3.3-4.6% with either cables or dumbbells [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable].

exercises.name: Cable fly (or pec deck)
exercises.summary: A chest [[term:isolation-exercise|isolation exercise]] that loads the pectorals in their stretched position, on a cable station or a pec-deck machine. From [[phase:p2]] it follows the main press on Upper A (10-15 reps, 60 s rest, in a [[term:superset|superset]]). Pulleys set low, sweeping up and in, probably bias the upper chest (anatomical inference).
setup: Cable: set both pulleys at their lowest point with D-handles, stand in the middle with one foot forward, chest up.
Pec deck: set the seat so the handles are at mid-chest and the arms start just behind your body line; note the setting in Hevy.
Elbows slightly bent and fixed, shoulder blades back.
execution: Sweep the handles up and in through a wide arc until they meet in front of your upper chest at about chin height (1-2 s).
Return for 2-3 s until you feel a firm stretch across the chest, hands just behind your body line and no further than your shoulders tolerate.
Keep the elbow angle the same throughout: a hug, not a press.
exercises.breathing: Out as the handles come together, in as they open; breathe continuously.
cues: Hug a large tree.
Bring the handles together in front of your chin.
Let the cables draw your arms wide before each rep.

errors.error: Bending and straightening the elbows, turning it into a press.
errors.fix: Fix the elbow bend and move only at the shoulder.

errors.error: Stretching so far back that you feel it in the front of the shoulder joint.
errors.fix: Stop at a firm chest stretch with your hands near your body line.

errors.error: Heavy weight with a short arc.
errors.fix: Lighten the load and use the whole arc.

exercises.startingLoad: A light pin you could move about 15 times; do 10-12 through the full arc in your first session. Log the station and pin.
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-10); letting go of the handles ends a set safely, so the last set may reach [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] over 10-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]), moving one pin step at the top of the range.
exercises.regression: Use the pec deck, which sets the path for you, or shorten the stretched end slightly if the shoulder complains ([[rule:pain]]).

alternatives.why: Free-weight chest work when no cable or pec deck is free.
A stable option, with less emphasis on the stretch.
Keeps the upper-chest bias with a press.

exercises.whyChosen: Adding an exercise that loads a muscle at a different length or region is the kind of variation that can add regional growth, whereas redundant variation adds nothing [@Kassiano2022_variationSR]. The fly loads the chest when stretched, which presses do less (inference).
exercises.safety: Keep the stretch comfortable: the shoulder is among the most often injured sites in weight training [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury]. To finish a cable set, bring the handles together first, then step back toward the stack before letting go.
exercises.mechanism: The fly is horizontal adduction alone: the pectoralis major does nearly all the work while the triceps only hold the elbow angle. Cables keep resistance at the stretched end, where a review argues hard loading produces the most growth [@Pedrosa2026_muscleLengthReview]; the low-to-high line follows the clavicular fibres (anatomical inference).
exercises.evidence: Pooled trials found only trivial differences in regional growth between training at longer and shorter muscle lengths (standardised effects 0.05-0.09) [@Varovic2025_lengthRegionalMeta], so treat the stretch emphasis as a sensible hedge rather than a proven multiplier. No located trial tests the fly itself for chest growth.

exercises.name: Overhead cable triceps extension
exercises.summary: An elbow-extension [[term:isolation-exercise|isolation exercise]] with your arms overhead, which puts the long head of the triceps on stretch. It joins Full body A from week 3 of [[phase:p1]] and stays on Upper A through [[phase:p4]] (10-15 reps, 60 s rest, in a [[term:superset|superset]]). The triceps are the larger part of the upper arm, so this is a core exercise for arm size.
setup: Attach a rope to the pulley at about head height or lower; grip the ends with palms facing each other.
Turn away from the stack into a staggered stance and lean slightly forward; a split stance suits you better than a deep hip hinge, given your tight hamstrings.
Raise your elbows beside your head, pointing forward, with your hands behind your head.
execution: Straighten your elbows until your arms point forward and up (about 1 s), spreading the rope ends slightly at the end.
Return for 2-3 s until your hands are well behind your head and you feel a deep stretch at the back of the upper arm.
Keep your upper arms still; only the forearms move.
exercises.breathing: Out as you extend, in as you return; breathe on every rep.
cues: Throw the rope ends forward toward the far wall.
Pull the rope apart at the end of each rep.
Let the rope sink deep behind your head before each rep.

errors.error: Elbows drifting wide and down.
errors.fix: Keep them pointing forward about shoulder-width apart; lighten the load if needed.

errors.error: Pressing with the shoulders.
errors.fix: Freeze the upper arms; only the elbows bend and straighten.

errors.error: Cutting the stretch short.
errors.fix: Let your hands travel fully behind your head on every rep.

errors.error: Struggling into position as the stack gets heavier.
errors.fix: Use the seated version: low pulley, sitting on a bench facing away from the stack.

exercises.startingLoad: A light pin you could move about 18 times, done for 12. You will use less weight than on a pushdown: in the key trial, overhead loads were 34-39% lower yet produced more growth [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps].
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-10); the last set may reach [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] over 10-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]), moving one pin step when every set reaches 15.
exercises.regression: Seated with a low pulley, or one arm at a time with a D-handle, left first. Without a free cable, hold one dumbbell overhead in both hands, seated with your back supported.

alternatives.why: Same muscle with the arms at your sides; less long-head stretch and less growth in a trial.
When no cable is free; a close hand position shifts work toward the triceps (inference).

exercises.whyChosen: In an MRI trial it grew the triceps clearly more than the arms-down version, at lighter loads, which makes it one of the better-supported selection choices in the programme ([[dec:D12]]).
exercises.safety: The deep stretch can irritate the elbow early on, so keep the first set light. Elbow pain that lingers into the next day: reduce the depth and see [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: The long head crosses the shoulder as well as the elbow, so raising the arm overhead lengthens it and the extension loads it at a long length; the lateral and medial heads cross only the elbow (anatomy). In the trial those single-joint heads also grew more overhead, so the benefit is not only about the long head [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps].
exercises.evidence: Overhead training increased whole-triceps volume by 19.9% versus 13.9% with the arm at the side (effect size d = 0.54): long head 28.5% vs 19.6%, lateral and medial heads 14.6% vs 10.5%, with similar strength gains [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps]. It is one trial of moderate certainty in untrained adults, with moderate effect sizes (d 0.39-0.61) that were consistent across the heads.

exercises.name: Cable triceps pushdown
equipment: cable station with bar or rope
exercises.summary: The arms-down triceps extension on a high cable: the triceps [[term:isolation-exercise|isolation exercise]] on Upper B in [[phase:p2]]-[[phase:p4]] (10-15 reps, 60 s rest, in a [[term:superset|superset]]), complementing the overhead extension on Upper A. It is simple to learn and safe to take close to failure.
setup: Attach a bar or rope to a high pulley; stand close with feet hip-width and a slight forward lean.
Pin your upper arms to your sides with the elbows bent to about 90°, wrists straight.
execution: Push the handle down until your elbows are fully straight (about 1 s); with a rope, spread the ends apart at the bottom.
Return for about 2 s until your forearms are just above parallel to the floor, elbows still at your sides.
Only the forearms move; reach full lockout on every rep.
exercises.breathing: Out as you push down, in on the way up; breathe on every rep.
cues: Push the handle down toward the floor.
Spread the rope ends to the outside of your thighs.
Keep the handle travelling close to your body.

errors.error: Elbows drifting forward so the shoulders join in.
errors.fix: Pin them to your sides and lighten the load.

errors.error: Leaning over the handle to push with bodyweight.
errors.fix: Stand taller, with only a slight lean.

errors.error: Stopping short of lockout.
errors.fix: Straighten fully on every rep.

exercises.startingLoad: A pin you could push about 18 times, done for 12. Log the pin and the attachment (bar or rope) in Hevy notes, as the numbers are not interchangeable.
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-10); the last set may reach [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] ([[dec:D07]]). It is a good exercise for checking your RIR guesses ([[rule:rir-calibration]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] over 10-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]), moving one pin step when every set reaches 15.
exercises.regression: A lighter pin with the rope, which many people find easier on the wrists and elbows (practical convention).

alternatives.why: Grew the triceps more in a trial; the priority triceps exercise.
When no cable is free; use a close hand position for the triceps (inference).
A [[phase:p3]] option that also loads the lower chest.

exercises.whyChosen: The overhead extension grows the triceps more, but pushdowns still grew them substantially in the same trial and add a second angle on the other upper-body day [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps]. Presses also train the triceps; counting such indirect sets as half a set fitted the dose-response data best [@Pelland2025_volume_frequency] (see [[term:fractional-sets|fractional set counting]]).
exercises.safety: Low risk. Keep your wrists straight; elbow pain that lingers between sessions: [[rule:pain]].
exercises.mechanism: With the arm at your side the long head is relatively short, so the lateral and medial heads do more of the work (anatomy), and the movement loads the triceps near full contraction rather than at a stretch.
exercises.evidence: With the arm at the side, whole-triceps volume rose 13.9%, against 19.9% overhead [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps]. In a study of trained and untrained men and women that included the pushdown, RIR predictions were more accurate closer to failure and in later sets, and training experience did not significantly affect accuracy [@Remmert2023_RIRtrainedUntrained].

exercises.name: Assisted dip
equipment: assisted dip machine or parallel bars
exercises.summary: A dip on parallel handles with a counterweight (or a band on bars) taking part of your bodyweight, for the lower chest and triceps. It is optional in [[phase:p3]]. Your shoulders set the depth: stop above any point that hurts.
setup: Select the counterweight (a higher number means more help), then step or kneel onto the platform and grip the handles at about shoulder width.
Start at the top with your arms straight, shoulders down away from your ears, torso leaning slightly forward.
execution: Lower for 2-3 s, bending the elbows and leaning slightly forward, until your upper arms are about parallel to the floor or you feel the first strain at the front of the shoulder, whichever comes first.
Press back up to straight arms (about 1 s) without shrugging.
Use the same depth on every rep.
exercises.breathing: In on the way down, out as you press up.
cues: Push the handles down into the floor.
Keep your shoulders far from your ears.
Lean toward the front of the machine as you lower.

errors.error: Sinking too deep with the shoulders rolling forward.
errors.fix: Stop with your upper arms parallel to the floor, or higher.

errors.error: Shrugging at the bottom.
errors.fix: Push the handles down to lift your chest.

errors.error: Bouncing out of the bottom.
errors.fix: Pause briefly, then press.

exercises.startingLoad: Choose assistance that allows 10-12 controlled reps with 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; even in [[phase:p3]] that may be a large share of your bodyweight (inference). Log the assistance value; a falling number is progress.
exercises.effort: Working sets end at 1-2 RIR (Hevy [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-9); stop before tired shoulders drift into the deep, rolled-forward position ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]): at the top of the range on every set, reduce the assistance by one step.
exercises.regression: More assistance or a shallower depth; or leave dips out and use [[ex:db-bench-press]].

alternatives.why: Chest and triceps without the deep shoulder extension.
Triceps only, and very shoulder-friendly.
Stable chest work.

exercises.whyChosen: It is optional because the presses already cover these muscles, and the bottom position stresses the front of the shoulder (practical convention). It suits [[phase:p3]], after two phases of pressing have built the strength and control it needs.
exercises.safety:
!> Stop at the depth where you feel no shoulder pain, and drop the exercise if pain persists ([[rule:pain]]). The shoulder is among the most often injured sites in weight training [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury].

Step off only once the platform has come to rest.
exercises.mechanism: Dips combine shoulder extension with elbow extension; the forward lean and the bottom position stretch the lower (sternocostal) chest. The counterweight subtracts from your bodyweight, so you set the load as on a machine.
exercises.evidence: No located trial tests dips for growth. Full range of motion generally gives larger strength gains (effect size 0.56) [@Pallares2021_ROMmeta], but pain sets the limit here, and partial ranges give only trivially smaller results overall (standardised effect 0.12 favouring full range) [@Wolf2023_partialFullMeta].

exercises.name: Lat pulldown
exercises.summary: A seated cable pull from overhead down to the top of your chest. It trains the latissimus dorsi and teres major, the muscles that give the back its width (the upper half of a V-taper). It is the machine version of the pull-up: you choose the load, so you can work in the 8-12 rep range now, while your pull-up is still at 3 reps, and push sets hard without a spotter.
setup: Fit a straight or wide bar. Set the thigh pad so your thighs are pinned with your feet flat on the floor.
Stand, take an overhand grip a little wider than your shoulders with thumbs wrapped round the bar, and sit down holding it.
Lean back about 10-15 degrees from vertical with your chest lifted.
Stacks in many Indian gyms are numbered rather than marked in kilograms, and no two pulldown machines feel alike: use the same machine each time and log the number shown (practical convention).
execution: Start with arms straight and shoulders allowed to rise toward your ears; this stretched position is part of every rep.
Pull the bar down in about 1 s to the top of your chest, elbows travelling down and slightly back toward your sides.
Touch or nearly touch your upper chest and pause briefly.
Return over 2-3 s until the arms are fully straight and the shoulders rise again; do not rest the stack between reps.
Keep the torso angle fixed. A rep you have to finish by swinging back does not count.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you pull, in as the bar rises. This lift needs no breath-hold.
cues: Pull the bar to the top of your chest along the line of the cable.
Try to bend the bar into a U as you pull.
Let the stack lift the bar all the way up before the next rep.
Keep the cable vertical: the bar should not drift forward or back.

errors.error: Leaning far back and rowing the bar to the stomach.
errors.fix: Reduce the load until every rep finishes with no more than a 10-15 degree lean; beyond that it becomes a row.

errors.error: Stopping short at the top with bent elbows.
errors.fix: Straighten the arms fully and let the shoulders rise each rep; the lats are longest, and most stretched under load, at the top.

errors.error: Pulling the bar behind the neck.
errors.fix: Pull in front of the face to the upper chest; behind-the-neck pulls force the shoulder into extreme rotation for no known benefit (practical convention).

errors.error: Yanking the weight down with body momentum.
errors.fix: Use a 1 s pull and a 2-3 s return; if you need momentum, the load is too heavy.

exercises.startingLoad: Use [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] ([[tool:warmup]]): 10 easy reps at a light setting, then add one or two plates per set until 10 reps would leave about 4 in reserve. A rough anchor for someone with a 3-rep pull-up is about half of body weight on the stack for 10 reps, but pulley friction and labelling vary so much that the reps, not the number, decide (inference).
exercises.effort: In the technique session ([[phase:p0]]) stop about 4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]], and in the first two weeks of [[phase:p1]] about 3-4. After that, end work sets at 1-2 RIR; the last set may go to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] because the machine lets you fail safely alone ([[dec:D07]]). In maintenance mode, where it is a main lift, use 2-3 RIR. People under-predict their remaining reps by about one on average [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy], so an occasional all-out last set is a useful check ([[rule:rir-calibration]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]): when all sets reach the top of the range at the target RIR (12 reps in [[phase:p1]], [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p4]]; 10 in [[phase:p3]] and [[phase:pm]]), add the smallest step the machine allows (often one plate of about 5 kg, or a 2.5 kg add-on weight) and build back up from the bottom of the range. From [[phase:p2]] the [[ex:pull-up]] becomes the main vertical pull and the pulldown adds volume.
exercises.regression: Lighten the stack, or swap to a neutral (parallel) grip handle, which many people find easier on the shoulders. A kneeling one-arm cable pulldown, left arm first, teaches the elbow path if the bar version feels awkward (practical convention).

alternatives.why: The same vertical pull with body weight; the main lift once you can do full sets.
Underhand vertical pull with more biceps involvement; a fair swap when the machine is busy.
If no vertical pull is free, a row still trains the lats and upper back, in a horizontal direction.

exercises.whyChosen: Back width is central to the athletic shape you want: in one perception study (95 British and Malaysian women rating images of men) a V-shaped torso was the main predictor of rated attractiveness in urban settings [@Swami2005_WCRcrossCultural]. The pulldown lets you load the vertical pull for hypertrophy before your pull-up can, it is quick to learn, and it is safe to push hard alone ([[dec:D08]]). It runs through every phase: the main vertical pull in [[phase:p1]] and maintenance, and extra back volume behind pull-ups in Phases 2-4.
exercises.safety: Keep the thigh pad snug so a heavy stack cannot lift you off the seat, and never let go of the bar at the bottom; guide it back to the top. If the front of the shoulder pinches at the top, narrow your grip or use a neutral handle, and stop for sharp pain ([[rule:pain]]). General rules for training alone: [[plan:safety]].
exercises.mechanism: The latissimus dorsi runs from the lower spine, pelvis and lower ribs to the front of the upper humerus, so it pulls the arm down and back toward the body (shoulder adduction and extension), helped by teres major. At the top of each rep the lats are at their longest, where passive tension in titin and connective tissue adds to active cross-bridge tension, one proposed input to [[term:mechanotransduction|mechanotransduction]] (hypothesis from general physiology, untested for this exercise). The biceps flex the elbow throughout, which is why a novice programme of only pulldowns and bench presses grew the elbow flexors by 6.5% in 10 weeks [@Gentil2013_singlejoint_addon].
exercises.evidence: No long-term trial compares vertical with horizontal pulling for back growth, so including both is inference. Lengthened-partial and full-range pulldowns gave similar 10RM gains in trained adults [@Wolf2025_LPupperPeerJ]; full [[term:rom|range of motion]] stays the default because it gave larger strength gains overall (effect size 0.56) [@Pallares2021_ROMmeta]. Machines and free weights produce similar hypertrophy ([[term:smd|SMD]] -0.055) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta]. [[term:superset|Supersets]] save time without reducing hypertrophy (SMD -0.05) [@Zhang2025_superset_meta], but in one 10-week trial they gave 5.2 kg less pulldown strength gain than traditional sets [@Iversen2024_superset_RCT].

exercises.name: Pull-up (with assisted and negative progressions)
exercises.summary: Hanging from a bar with an overhand grip and pulling until your chin clears it. It trains the same back muscles as the pulldown, but it is also a skill, moving your own body through space, which carries over to climbing, martial arts and general athleticism. Your baseline is 3 reps, so the programme builds it in stages: frequent low-rep practice sets and slow lowering (negatives), then full sets with assistance where needed, then added load.
setup: Stand on a box or bench under the bar so you can grip it without jumping. Wipe the bar and dry your hands; in midday heat, sweat makes grip the first thing to fail.
Overhand grip a little wider than your shoulders, thumbs round the bar.
Step off into a dead hang: arms straight, legs together and slightly in front, glutes and abdominals lightly tensed so you do not swing.
Assisted machine: kneel or stand on the platform; more counterweight means more help. Band: loop it over the bar and put one knee or foot in it.
execution: From the dead hang, pull your chest toward the bar until your chin clears it, taking 1-2 s.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower over 2-3 s to straight arms; every rep starts from a full hang.
Negatives: step up from the box until your chin is over the bar, then lower yourself over 3-5 s to a dead hang. Step back up; do not pull.
End the set by stepping back onto the box, not by dropping.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in at the bottom, brace lightly, and breathe out as you pass the hardest part near the top. Do not hold your breath through a whole set.
cues: Pull the bar down to your chest.
Try to bend the bar into a U.
Drive your chest up to the bar.
Keep your feet pointing at the same spot on the floor.

errors.error: Half reps: arms never straight at the bottom, or chin stopping below the bar.
errors.fix: Count only reps from a dead hang to chin over the bar; use assistance to keep the full range rather than shortening it.

errors.error: Kicking or swinging to get up.
errors.fix: Keep the legs together and still; if you need a kick, the set is over.

errors.error: Negatives that turn into a drop.
errors.fix: Count 3-5 s down. If you cannot slow the descent, do negatives on the assisted machine.

errors.error: Grinding every practice set to failure.
errors.fix: In Phase 1, stop with 2 or more reps left: frequent, fresh reps build the skill faster than exhausted ones (practical convention).

exercises.startingLoad: Body weight for practice sets of 1-3 reps. On the assisted machine, choose the counterweight that lets you hit the session's rep target with 2-3 reps in reserve, and reduce it as you get stronger. In Hevy, log assisted sets as 'Pull Up (Assisted)' with the counterweight, and negatives under 'Pull Up' with a note such as 'neg 4 s' ([[plan:logging]]).
exercises.effort: [[phase:p1]]: practice sets ending with at least 2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; the aim is skill, not fatigue. From [[phase:p2]]: work sets at 1-2 RIR (2-3 in maintenance mode, where it is a main lift). Avoid true failure on unassisted sets, since a failed rep leaves you hanging with no spotter. Sets taken to failure cause more fatigue and feel worse [@Refalo2023_proximityFatigue; @Refalo2025_proximityPerceptual], and in a trial in trained lifters gave no more growth than stopping 1-2 reps short [@Refalo2024_FAILvsRIRhypertrophy].
exercises.progression:
1. Practice ([[phase:p1]], Full body B): 1-3 reps per set, 90 s rest. When all sets feel easy, add a rep to each. From week 3, finish with 1-2 negatives.
2. At 3 x 5 strict reps: move to sets of 5-8, keeping the 2-rep margin.
3. From [[phase:p2]]: use the rep range the session shows. If body weight alone falls below the bottom of the range, do the remaining sets assisted, with the least counterweight that works.
4. When all sets pass the top of the range: add load with a dip belt or a dumbbell held between the feet, 2.5 kg at a time.

Each stage uses [[term:double-progression|double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]); stalls follow [[rule:stall]].
exercises.regression: Assisted pull-ups (machine or band), negatives only, or the [[ex:lat-pulldown]]. On a day when you cannot complete a rep, do 3 dead hangs of 20-30 s plus negatives (practical convention).

alternatives.why: Same muscles with adjustable load; use it when the bar is busy or for extra volume.
Underhand grip; most people manage a rep or two more, so it works as a stepping stone or a variation.

exercises.whyChosen: The pull-up is both a test ([[ex:test-pullup]]) and a real-world strength skill. Strength gains are largely specific to the movement practised: in a meta-analysis, dynamic training raised strength in the trained task about twice as much as untrained isometric strength ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.98 vs 0.42) [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta]. So you practise the pull-up itself rather than hoping the pulldown carries over. It is the main vertical pull from [[phase:p2]] onward and in maintenance ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: Use a box to get on and off the bar and step down rather than dropping, especially with tired hands. Unaccustomed exercise is a recognised trigger of [[term:rhabdomyolysis|exertional rhabdomyolysis]] [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo], and weightlifting accounts for about 15% of reported cases [@Backer2022_exertionalRhabdoSR]; lots of slow negatives in your first weeks is exactly that kind of exercise (inference), so keep them to 1-3 per session at first. Seek same-day care for muscle pain or swelling far beyond normal soreness, marked weakness or dark urine ([[plan:safety]]). Stop for sharp elbow or shoulder pain ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: The pull-up uses the same actions as the pulldown (shoulder adduction and extension by the lats and teres major, elbow flexion by the biceps and brachialis), but your body moves instead of the bar, so the trunk must stay stiff and the grip must hold your whole body weight. Early strength gains in a new movement are attributed mainly to [[term:neural-adaptation|neural adaptation]], such as higher motor-unit discharge rates and better coordination [@Skarabot2021_neural_review], which is why frequent, fresh, low-rep practice comes first. Negatives work because a muscle can control more load while lengthening than it can lift (general physiology).
exercises.evidence: No trial located compares pull-up progression methods; the staged approach is practical convention. Supporting points: strength is task-specific [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta]; shorter and longer lowering phases gave similar hypertrophy (g 0.05) and an uncertain strength difference [@Amdi2025_eccentric_duration], so negatives are a bridge to full reps rather than a superior stimulus; and stopping 1-2 reps short of failure gave similar growth with less fatigue [@Refalo2024_FAILvsRIRhypertrophy; @Refalo2023_proximityFatigue].

exercises.name: Chin-up
exercises.summary: A pull-up with palms facing you and hands about shoulder-width apart. The underhand grip puts the biceps in a stronger line of pull, so most people manage a rep or two more than with an overhand grip (practical convention). It replaces the pulldown in Upper A for the first eight weeks of [[phase:p3]] (6-10 reps, 90 s rest).
setup: Box under the bar; dry your hands and the bar.
Underhand grip, hands about shoulder-width apart, thumbs round the bar.
Dead hang with legs together and slightly in front, abdominals and glutes lightly tensed.
execution: Pull in 1-2 s until your chin clears the bar, elbows travelling down in front of your body.
Pause briefly, then lower over 2-3 s to fully straight arms.
Finish the set by stepping back onto the box.
exercises.breathing: Breathe in at the bottom and out as you pass the top half of the rep; no breath-hold across the set.
cues: Pull the bar to your upper chest.
Keep your feet pointing at one spot on the floor.
Lower until the bar pulls your arms straight.

errors.error: Craning the chin up to clear the bar.
errors.fix: Keep the head level; the rep counts when the chin passes the bar without reaching.

errors.error: Partial reps at the bottom.
errors.fix: Start every rep from straight arms; use assistance rather than cutting the range.

errors.error: Wrist or inner-elbow ache from the fully turned grip.
errors.fix: Use a neutral (parallel) grip on the same bar, or the pulldown with a neutral handle (practical convention).

exercises.startingLoad: Body weight. If the first set falls short of 6 reps, use the assisted machine or a band with the least help that gets you into 6-10 reps at 1-2 reps in reserve; log it under 'Chin Up' with the counterweight in the notes.
exercises.effort: Work sets at 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. Avoid true failure: a failed rep leaves you hanging with no spotter, and stopping 1-2 reps short gave similar growth to failure in a trial in trained lifters [@Refalo2024_FAILvsRIRhypertrophy].
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 6-10 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). When all sets reach 10, add 2.5 kg with a dip belt or a dumbbell held between the feet; if you are still assisted, reduce the counterweight by one step instead.
exercises.regression: Assisted chin-ups, negatives (3-5 s lowering), or an underhand-grip [[ex:lat-pulldown]].

alternatives.why: Overhand version; the main vertical pull in Upper B.
Loadable machine version; returns to Upper A from week 9 of Phase 3.

exercises.whyChosen: Planned variation: [[phase:p3]] swaps the pulldown for chin-ups for eight weeks, then switches back. A systematic review found that reasoned variation (a new grip, region or muscle emphasis) can help, while frequent random rotation may blunt gains [@Kassiano2022_variationSR]. The underhand grip also gives the biceps more work inside a back exercise (practical convention).
exercises.safety: As for the pull-up: box on and off, no dropping from the bar, and stop for sharp elbow or wrist pain ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: The biceps brachii both flexes the elbow and turns the palm up (supination); with the palm already up it pulls with its full strength, while a palm-down grip partly disadvantages it (general anatomy). The elbows travel in front of the body rather than out to the sides, so the lats work more through shoulder extension than adduction (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: No trial has compared chin-ups with pull-ups for hypertrophy. In novices, compound pulling alone grew the elbow flexors (6.5% vs 7.0% with added curls) [@Gentil2013_singlejoint_addon], though in a direct comparison a curl grew them about twice as much as a row (11.1% vs 5.2%) [@Mannarino2021_curl_vs_row]. Strength is specific to the trained movement [@Saeterbakken2025_taskSpecificityMeta], so your chin-up and pull-up numbers will move somewhat independently.

exercises.name: Seated cable row
exercises.summary: A horizontal pull on a low cable: sitting with feet braced, you pull a V-handle to your lower ribs. It trains the mid-back (middle trapezius, rhomboids) and lats, adding thickness to the upper back and balancing your pressing. It is the row in the technique session ([[phase:p0]]), Full body B ([[phase:p1]]), Upper B ([[phase:p2]], [[phase:p4]]) and maintenance.
setup: Attach the V-handle and sit with your feet on the platform.
Your hamstrings are tight, so bend your knees as much as you need to sit with the pelvis upright and the lower back neutral. Straight legs would tip the pelvis back and round the lower back.
Sit back until the arms are straight and the weight is lifted off the stack, torso upright.
execution: Start with arms straight and shoulder blades drawn forward by the handle; a 10-15 degree forward lean is fine.
Pull the handle to your lower ribs in about 1 s, elbows close to the body, and pause 1 s with your chest tall.
Return over 2-3 s until the arms are straight and the shoulder blades have moved forward again.
The torso moves only slightly; the arms and shoulder blades do the work.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you pull, in on the return.
cues: Pull the handle to your belt line.
Drive the handle straight back along the cable.
Let the cable pull your arms long before each rep.
Keep the stack hovering between reps.

errors.error: Rocking the torso to move the weight.
errors.fix: Lighten the load; lean no more than 10-15 degrees either way.

errors.error: Rounded lower back from sitting with straight legs.
errors.fix: Bend the knees more and sit tall.

errors.error: Shrugging the handle up toward the chest.
errors.fix: Pull back at belt-line height, not up.

errors.error: Cutting the return short.
errors.fix: Let the arms straighten fully and the shoulder blades move forward each rep.

exercises.startingLoad: Ramp up from a light setting: 10 reps, then add one or two plates per set until 10 reps leave about 4 in reserve. Log the machine and the stack number shown, since labelling varies between gyms.
exercises.effort: About 4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] in the technique session and 3-4 in weeks 1-2, then 1-2 RIR; the last set can approach [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] because the stack simply returns. In maintenance mode, where it is a main lift, use 2-3 RIR. It suits the occasional calibration set in [[rule:rir-calibration]]: in a trial that included the seated row, predictions became more accurate closer to failure, and training experience made no significant difference [@Remmert2023_RIRtrainedUntrained].
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] ([[rule:double-progression]]): 8-12 reps in Phases 1, 2 and 4, 6-10 in maintenance. When all sets reach the top of the range, add one plate and build back up.
exercises.regression: Lighter load, or the [[ex:chest-supported-row]] if your lower back tires or rounds.

alternatives.why: Removes the lower-back and hamstring demand completely.
Free-weight row, one side at a time.

exercises.whyChosen: A horizontal row complements the vertical pull; no trial has compared the two directions for back growth, so including both is low-cost inference. The cable keeps tension through the whole range, failure is safe alone, and the row pairs naturally with a press in a [[term:superset|superset]] ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: Low risk. Keep the lower back neutral, which with your hamstrings means bent knees. At the end of a heavy set, lean forward and return the handle to the stack rather than letting it snap forward.
exercises.mechanism: With the elbows close to the sides, the lats extend the shoulder while the middle trapezius and rhomboids pull the shoulder blades together. Letting the blades travel forward at the start lengthens those retractors, so the full range loads them from stretched to shortened (biomechanical reasoning). The biceps flex the elbow throughout, so a row counts as partial biceps work ([[term:fractional-sets|fractional set counting]]).
exercises.evidence: Machines and free weights produce similar hypertrophy ([[term:smd|SMD]] -0.055) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], and full [[term:rom|range of motion]] gave larger strength gains than partial range (effect size 0.56) [@Pallares2021_ROMmeta]. Supersets matched traditional sets for hypertrophy in less time [@Zhang2025_superset_meta], but in one 10-week trial the superset group gained 4.8 kg less on the seated row (p = 0.073, not significant) [@Iversen2024_superset_RCT]. A dumbbell row grew the elbow flexors about half as much as curls (5.2% vs 11.1%) [@Mannarino2021_curl_vs_row].

exercises.name: Chest-supported row
equipment: incline bench and dumbbells, or T-bar/row machine
exercises.summary: Lying face down on an incline bench (or against a row machine's chest pad) and rowing two dumbbells up to your sides. The support removes any need to hold your trunk in position, so the upper back can be worked hard with no lower-back or hamstring demand. It is the row in Upper A in [[phase:p2]] to [[phase:p4]] (8-12 reps in a [[term:superset|superset]], 60 s rest).
setup: Set an adjustable bench to 30-45 degrees and place the dumbbells beside its front end.
Lie face down with your chest on the top of the pad and chin just past the end; feet braced on the floor, knees bent as comfortable.
Pick up the dumbbells and let your arms hang straight, palms facing each other.
Machine version: set the chest pad so you reach the handles with arms straight and shoulder blades spread.
execution: Row the dumbbells up and back toward your hips in about 1 s until the elbows pass the torso.
