Pause 1 s at the top with your chest still on the pad.
Lower over 2-3 s to full arm extension, letting the shoulder blades spread apart.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you row, in as you lower. The pad presses on your chest, so keep breaths short and steady.
cues: Keep your chest glued to the pad.
Row the dumbbells toward your back pockets.
Let the dumbbells hang toward the floor at the bottom of every rep.

errors.error: Lifting the chest off the pad to finish reps.
errors.fix: Reduce the load; the support is the point of the exercise.

errors.error: Short range, with the arms never fully straight.
errors.fix: Let the arms straighten and the shoulder blades spread at the bottom.

errors.error: Shrugging the dumbbells toward the ears.
errors.fix: Row toward the hips, not toward the shoulders.

errors.error: Cranking the neck up to look ahead.
errors.fix: Keep the head in line with the spine, eyes on the floor.

exercises.startingLoad: Dumbbells you could row about 15 times, often 7.5-12.5 kg each for an untrained man (practical convention). Adjust by the smallest step on your rack, usually 2.5 kg.
exercises.effort: About 3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] in the first session or two while you learn it, then 2-3 RIR with dumbbells, as for other free-weight compound lifts, never to failure alone ([[dec:D07]]). On a chest-pad machine, 1-2 RIR, and the last set may reach [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]].
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 8-12 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). A 2.5 kg jump per hand is large at these weights, so expect to fall back to 8-9 reps after each increase.
exercises.regression: Lighter dumbbells, a chest-pad row machine, or the [[ex:seated-cable-row]].

alternatives.why: Cable version with constant tension and only a small lower-back demand.
Bench-supported, one side at a time; use it if no incline bench is free.

exercises.whyChosen: Chest support keeps fatigue off your lower back, which squats and Romanian deadlifts already load during the week, and sidesteps your tight hamstrings (inference). It sets up quickly beside a press for a superset; pairing opposing muscles even increased the reps completed in a meta-analysis ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.68) [@Zhang2025_superset_meta] ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: Very low risk. Pick the dumbbells up from the floor beside the bench and set them down at the end rather than dropping them: weights dropping on the person were the commonest injury mechanism (65.5%) in emergency-department data on weight training [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED].
exercises.mechanism: Same muscles as other rows: the lats extend the shoulder, the middle trapezius and rhomboids retract the shoulder blades, and the rear deltoids assist. With the trunk supported, the spinal erectors no longer have to hold a forward lean, so more of each set's effort goes to the target muscles (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: A prone (chest-supported) row was one of four lifts in a matched trial in trained men in which free-weight and machine programmes gave similar strength gains and similar growth in the muscles measured, with differences of 2% or less [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT]; across trials, equipment type barely changes hypertrophy (SMD -0.055) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta]. Supersets matched traditional sets for hypertrophy (SMD -0.05) while saving time [@Zhang2025_superset_meta].

exercises.name: One-arm dumbbell row
exercises.summary: Rowing one dumbbell at a time with the other hand and knee braced on a bench. It is a free-weight row that trains each side separately and lets the shoulder blade move freely for a long stretch at the bottom. It replaces the cable row in Upper B in [[phase:p3]] (8-12 reps per side, in a [[term:superset|superset]], 90 s rest).
setup: Dumbbell on the floor beside the bench. Put your right knee and right hand on the bench, left foot on the floor slightly back and out to the side: the left arm works first.
Torso roughly parallel to the floor with a flat back. With your tight hamstrings, bend the standing knee as much as you need to keep the lower back neutral.
Pick up the dumbbell with a bent standing knee and let it hang straight below the shoulder.
execution: Row the dumbbell up and back toward your hip in about 1 s, elbow close to your side, and pause 1 s when the elbow passes the torso.
Lower over 2-3 s to a straight arm, letting the shoulder blade drop toward the floor for the stretch.
Do all reps on the left, then the same number on the right.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you row, in as you lower.
cues: Row the dumbbell toward your back pocket.
Keep your back as still as a tabletop.
Push the bench away with your supporting hand.
Let the dumbbell pull your arm long toward the floor at the bottom.

errors.error: Twisting the torso to heave the weight up.
errors.fix: Lighten the load; the torso stays still and roughly level.

errors.error: Pulling to the chest with the elbow flared out.
errors.fix: Aim the dumbbell at your hip so the lats do the work.

errors.error: Rounded lower back from a straight-legged stance.
errors.fix: Bend the standing knee and shorten the stance.

errors.error: Doing extra reps on the stronger right side.
errors.fix: The left side sets the reps; match them on the right (practical convention).

exercises.startingLoad: A dumbbell you could row about 15 times; 10-15 kg is a common start for an untrained man (practical convention). Use the same dumbbell for both sides.
exercises.effort: 2-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] on the left, as for other free-weight compound lifts ([[dec:D07]]); match those reps on the right even if it could do more.
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 8-12 reps per side ([[rule:double-progression]]); move up one dumbbell step (often 2.5 kg) when both sides reach 12 on all sets.
exercises.regression: A lighter dumbbell, or the [[ex:chest-supported-row]] if bracing on the bench is the limiting factor.

alternatives.why: Two-handed cable row with a simpler set-up.
Both arms at once with the trunk fully supported.

exercises.whyChosen: It is the planned [[phase:p3]] variation on the cable row ([[dec:D08]]): a free-weight row with a long stretch at the bottom and a small anti-rotation demand on the trunk. Working one side at a time also exposes any left-right difference, and starting with the left follows the programme's left-first convention ([[dec:D28]]).
exercises.safety: Low risk. Pick the dumbbell up and put it down with a bent-knee, flat-back movement rather than a straight-legged reach, which your hamstrings will not allow comfortably.
exercises.mechanism: Same muscles as other rows. A single dumbbell lets the shoulder blade travel further forward at the bottom than a bar or a two-handed attachment, lengthening the lats and mid-back at the start of each rep (biomechanical reasoning). The biceps work too, but less than in a curl.
exercises.evidence: In one RCT, a unilateral dumbbell row grew the elbow flexors 5.2% versus 11.1% for curls, and 10RM gains were specific to the exercise trained [@Mannarino2021_curl_vs_row]. [[term:unilateral|Unilateral]] and bilateral training showed no difference in hypertrophy, while strength follows the mode trained (unilateral strength g 0.42 in favour of unilateral training) [@Kassiano2025_uniVsBiMeta; @Xin2026_uniVsBiMultilevel]. Free weights and machines grow muscle equally [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta].

exercises.name: Face pull
exercises.summary: Pulling a rope from a high cable toward your face while rotating your hands back. It trains the rear deltoids, the rotator-cuff muscles that turn the arm outward, and the middle trapezius. It is light, high-rep isolation work (12-20 reps, 45 s rest) in Upper B in [[phase:p2]] to [[phase:p4]].
setup: Set the pulley at forehead height or slightly higher and attach a rope.
Grip the rope ends with thumbs pointing back toward you.
Step back until the arms are straight and the weight is off the stack; feet staggered, slight lean back.
execution: Pull the rope toward your forehead in about 1 s, elbows high (about shoulder height) and wide.
As the rope reaches your face, pull the ends apart and rotate your hands back so the knuckles point behind you; hold 1 s.
Return over 2 s until the arms are straight.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you pull, in on the return.
cues: Pull the rope to your forehead and split it apart.
Finish with the rope ends beside your ears.
Point your knuckles at the wall behind you at the end of each rep.

errors.error: Too heavy, turning it into a leaning row.
errors.fix: Drop the load until you can hold the end position for 1 s.

errors.error: Elbows dropping below the hands.
errors.fix: Keep the elbows at shoulder height and wide; raise the pulley if needed.

errors.error: No rotation at the end.
errors.fix: Split the rope and turn the knuckles back; that rotation is what trains the external rotators.

exercises.startingLoad: Light: the lightest setting or one above it, aiming for 15-20 reps with 2-3 in reserve. These muscles handle far less load than rows do.
exercises.effort: Take sets to about 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. Effort matters with light loads: at 30% of [[term:1rm|1RM]], sets to failure grew the quadriceps 7.8% versus 2.8% for sets stopped well short [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load]. RIR estimates are least accurate in sets above 12 reps [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy], so judge by the reps slowing and by the rep target.
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 12-20 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). Stack jumps are large relative to the load; if the next plate drops you below 12 reps, stay at the current weight and add reps first (practical convention).
exercises.regression: Lighter load, a seated face pull to stop leaning, or band pull-aparts.

alternatives.why: Machine rear-delt work with simpler technique; the Upper A rear-delt exercise.
Band-only version for when no cable is free.

exercises.whyChosen: Rear deltoids complete the rounded look of the shoulder and get little direct work from presses ([[dec:D12]]). Adding external rotation to balance the programme's pressing is practical convention; that it prevents shoulder injury has not been tested (inference), although the shoulder is among the most commonly injured sites in weight-training sports [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury].
exercises.safety: Very low risk. Stop for pain or pinching at the front or top of the shoulder as the hands rise; lower the pulley and reduce the rotation.
exercises.mechanism: The rear deltoid draws the arm backward in the horizontal plane (horizontal abduction); infraspinatus and teres minor rotate the upper arm outward (external rotation); the middle trapezius pulls the shoulder blades together. One movement trains all three with modest loads (functional anatomy).
exercises.evidence: No trial located tests face pulls specifically. Hypertrophy is similar with light (more than 15RM), moderate (9-15RM) and heavy (8RM or less) loads when sets are taken to failure [@Lopez2021_load_NMA], which justifies high reps for small muscles that are awkward to load heavily. An external focus of attention, on the rope rather than the muscles, improves performance (g 0.26) and learning [@Chua2021_externalFocusMA].

exercises.name: Reverse pec deck (rear-delt fly)
exercises.summary: Sitting facing the pec-deck pad and sweeping the handles out and back with nearly straight arms. It isolates the rear deltoids, helped by the middle trapezius and rhomboids. It is the rear-delt exercise in Upper A from [[phase:p2]] to [[phase:p4]] (12-20 reps, 45 s rest).
setup: Set the machine arms to the rear-delt position and the seat so the handles are at shoulder height.
Sit facing the pad, chest against it, and grip the handles with palms facing each other or down.
Arms reach forward with a slight, fixed bend at the elbow.
Dumbbell version: lie face down on a 30-45 degree incline bench and make the same movement.
execution: Sweep the handles out and back in a wide arc in about 1 s until your arms are in line with your body; do not go far behind it.
Pause 1 s.
Return over 2 s until the stack nearly touches, then start the next rep.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you sweep back, in as you return.
cues: Push the handles out toward the side walls.
Make the widest arc you can with the handles.
Keep the handles at shoulder height all the way.

errors.error: Bending and straightening the elbows, turning it into a row.
errors.fix: Fix a slight elbow bend and keep it; the movement happens only at the shoulder.

errors.error: Shrugging and jamming the shoulder blades together.
errors.fix: Think wide rather than back (practical convention).

errors.error: Using momentum with a load that is too heavy.
errors.fix: Use a 2 s return and a pause at the back; if you cannot pause, reduce the load.

exercises.startingLoad: The lightest or second-lightest setting, aiming for 15-20 reps with 2-3 in reserve. With dumbbells, 2.5-5 kg each is a usual start (practical convention).
exercises.effort: Take sets to 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]], judged by the last reps slowing; failure is safe on this machine. With light loads, getting close to failure is what makes the set effective [@Lasevicius2022_failure_by_load], and RIR estimates are poor above 12 reps [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy].
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 12-20 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). If the next plate is too big a jump, add reps toward 20 first, or use a small add-on weight if the machine has one (practical convention).
exercises.regression: Lighter load, the incline dumbbell version, or band pull-aparts.

alternatives.why: Cable version that adds external rotation; the Upper B rear-delt exercise.
Band version for when the machine is in use.

exercises.whyChosen: Rear deltoids complete the three-dimensional shoulder of an athletic frame, and the machine makes them easy to load and safe to push hard alone. Upper A uses this and Upper B uses the [[ex:face-pull]], so both get a weekly turn ([[dec:D12]]).
exercises.safety: Very low risk. Stop for pain at the front or top of the shoulder and shorten the backward range.
exercises.mechanism: With the arm in front at shoulder height, sweeping it out and back is horizontal abduction, the rear deltoid's main action, while the middle trapezius and rhomboids steady and retract the shoulder blades. A machine's cam spreads resistance more evenly across the arc than a dumbbell, which is heaviest when the arm is horizontal (biomechanical reasoning).
exercises.evidence: No trial located compares rear-delt exercises. For the neighbouring lateral deltoid, cable and dumbbell raises gave equal growth (3.3-4.6% thickness) [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable], and across studies machines and free weights grow muscle equally [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta], so use whichever version is free. Light, high-rep sets grow muscle as well as heavy ones when taken to failure [@Lopez2021_load_NMA; @Schoenfeld2017_load_meta].

exercises.name: Incline dumbbell curl
exercises.summary: Curling dumbbells while lying back on an incline bench, arms hanging behind your torso. This position stretches the biceps across the shoulder, so every rep starts with the muscle long. It joins Full body A from week 3 of [[phase:p1]] and is the Upper A curl in [[phase:p2]], [[phase:p4]] and the last weeks of [[phase:p3]] (10-15 reps, 60 s rest).
setup: Set the bench to 45-60 degrees and sit back with your head and upper back on the pad, feet flat.
Let the arms hang straight down from the shoulders, slightly behind the torso, palms facing forward.
If the front of the shoulder feels strained in this stretch, raise the bench angle.
execution: Curl both dumbbells, or alternate starting with the left, in about 1 s, keeping the upper arm still and pointing at the floor.
Stop when the forearm is near vertical, before the dumbbell rests on your shoulder; pause briefly.
Lower over 2-3 s to fully straight elbows, without bouncing.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out on the curl, in on the way down. Near failure keep breathing rather than holding your breath: a single-arm curl to failure produced a mean peak blood pressure of 255/190 mmHg, partly from breath-holding ([[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]]) [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting].
cues: Lift the dumbbells in a smooth arc in front of the bench.
Let the dumbbells hang straight down to the floor between reps.
Keep the bench pad touching your shoulders throughout.

errors.error: Swinging the elbows forward to lift the weight.
errors.fix: Keep the upper arm hanging and still; use lighter dumbbells.

errors.error: Cutting the bottom of the range short.
errors.fix: Straighten the elbows fully every rep; the stretched start is the reason for this exercise.

errors.error: Shoulders lifting off the pad as you tire.
errors.fix: Keep head and shoulders on the bench; reduce the load.

exercises.startingLoad: Lighter than a standing curl: 5-7.5 kg per hand is a common start (practical convention), adjusted so 12-15 reps leave 2-3 in reserve.
exercises.effort: After the first two weeks, 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; stop at 0 RIR rather than failing a rep, since the programme keeps [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] for machines and cables ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 10-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). Going from 7.5 to 10 kg is a third heavier, so expect to restart near 10 reps; if your rack has 1 kg steps at the light end, use them.
exercises.regression: Raise the bench angle (less stretch), use lighter dumbbells, or do a seated dumbbell curl.

alternatives.why: Constant cable tension and smaller load steps.
Also loads the elbow flexors near full extension, with the upper arm fixed on a pad.
Neutral grip that shifts work to the brachialis and brachioradialis.

exercises.whyChosen: Arms are part of the athletic look you want. The incline curl loads the biceps at a long length, a low-cost hedge on the hypothesis that exercises loading a muscle in its stretched position grow it more [@Pedrosa2026_muscleLengthReview]. For the biceps the direct evidence is mixed, so this is a hedge, not a proven advantage ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: Low risk. The stretched bottom position loads the front of the shoulder and the biceps tendon: lower under control, never bounce, and raise the bench angle if the front of the shoulder hurts ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: The long head of the biceps crosses both shoulder and elbow. With the arm hanging behind the torso (shoulder extended) it is lengthened at the shoulder, so it works at a longer length throughout the curl (functional anatomy). The same lever, lengthening a two-joint muscle at its second joint, grew the triceps about 1.4 times more with overhead extensions [@Maeo2023_overheadTriceps]; for the biceps the results so far are mixed.
exercises.evidence: Low-load occluded curls with the biceps short or long produced similar growth over 3 weeks (+8.5% vs +7.4% at 85% of humerus length) [@Vendruscolo2024_curlShoulderPosition], and lengthened partials matched full range for elbow-flexor growth [@Wolf2025_LPupperPeerJ]. Curls grew the elbow flexors about twice as much as rows (11.1% vs 5.2%) [@Mannarino2021_curl_vs_row]. Responses vary widely: biceps size changes in one study ranged from -2% to +59% [@Hubal2005_variability]. On isolation exercises an internal focus ('squeeze the biceps') also has support: it gave more elbow-flexor growth than an external focus (12.4% vs 6.9%) in one RCT [@Schoenfeld2018_attentionalFocusHypertrophy].

exercises.name: Preacher curl
equipment: preacher bench with EZ bar/dumbbell or machine
exercises.summary: Curling with your upper arms resting on an angled pad. The pad fixes the upper arm in front of you so you cannot swing, and the resistance is heaviest early in the lift, when the elbow is nearly straight and the elbow flexors are long. It is the Upper B curl in [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p4]] (10-15 reps, 60 s rest).
setup: Machine: adjust the seat so your armpits sit snugly over the top of the pad and the backs of your upper arms lie flat on it, elbows level with the machine's pivot.
Free-weight version: an EZ bar with a shoulder-width grip on the angled parts, or one dumbbell at a time, left arm first.
execution: Curl up in about 1 s until the forearms are near vertical; pause briefly.
Lower over 2-3 s to just short of a locked elbow, keeping full control through the last part.
Reverse smoothly at the bottom, with no drop or bounce.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out on the curl, in on the way down; keep breathing through the final reps.
cues: Press the pad down with the backs of your arms.
Lower the handle as if setting it gently on a shelf.
Move the handle in a smooth arc at the same speed every rep.

errors.error: Bouncing out of the bottom.
errors.fix: Slow the last third of the lowering and reverse smoothly.

errors.error: Elbows lifting off the pad, or rising from the seat.
errors.fix: Reduce the load; the arms stay in contact with the pad.

errors.error: Seat too high or low, so the pad does not support the upper arm.
errors.fix: Adjust until the armpits sit over the top of the pad.

errors.error: Curling the wrists to finish reps.
errors.fix: Keep the wrists straight, in line with the forearms.

exercises.startingLoad: The lightest plate or two on the machine, or a lightly loaded EZ bar, ramped up until 12-15 reps leave 2-3 in reserve.
exercises.effort: 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] once you are past the first two weeks; on the machine, failure is safe. Avoid grinding a failed rep at the very bottom, the most strained position for the elbow (practical convention).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 10-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]), using the smallest available step (add-on weights on the machine, 1.25 kg plates on an EZ bar).
exercises.regression: Lighter load; a slightly shorter bottom range for a week or two if the elbow is irritated; or the [[ex:cable-curl]].

alternatives.why: Also loads the biceps long; the Upper A curl.
Standing cable curl with constant tension, for when the preacher is taken.

exercises.whyChosen: With the upper arm fixed, all the work falls on the elbow flexors, and the resistance peaks where the muscles are long, the same low-cost hedge as the incline curl [@Pedrosa2026_muscleLengthReview]. Removing the swing also makes your reps-in-reserve judgements cleaner when training alone ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: The elbow is one of the most commonly injured sites in weight-training sports [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury]. The bottom of a preacher curl puts the most strain on the biceps tendon (practical convention): control the lowering, stop a few degrees short of lockout under heavy load, and stop for sharp pain at the front of the elbow ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: With the upper arm on a pad sloping away from you, the weight's lever arm about the elbow is greatest early in the lift, when the forearm passes horizontal with the elbow only slightly bent, and falls to almost nothing at the top. A standing curl is the reverse: hardest at 90 degrees and nearly unloaded at the bottom. So the preacher curl loads the elbow flexors mostly in their lengthened range (biomechanical reasoning); a machine's cam can alter this profile.
exercises.evidence: In trained lifters, preacher curls done only in the lengthened half of the range matched full-range preacher curls for growth (trivially more at 70% of humeral length, [[term:smd|SMD]] 0.10), while full range gave slightly better 1RM (SMD 0.17) [@Havers2025_preacherLP]. Full range remains the default because, across trials, every outcome slightly favoured it (SMD 0.05-0.2) [@Wolf2023_partialFullMeta]. Curls grew the elbow flexors about twice as much as rows [@Mannarino2021_curl_vs_row].

exercises.name: Cable curl
exercises.summary: A standing curl on a low pulley with a straight or EZ bar. The cable keeps tension on the biceps at the bottom of the range, where a dumbbell curl is almost unloaded, and the stack allows small load steps. It is the Upper A curl for the first 16 weeks of [[phase:p3]] (10-15 reps, 60 s rest), before the incline dumbbell curl returns.
setup: Set the pulley at its lowest position and attach a straight or EZ bar.
Stand about half a step back from the pulley, feet hip-width, knees soft, trunk lightly braced.
Underhand grip at shoulder width; arms straight, elbows at your sides.
execution: Curl the bar up in about 1 s, elbows staying near your sides.
Pause briefly when the forearms are near vertical.
Lower over 2-3 s to fully straight arms without letting the stack touch down.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out on the curl, in on the way down.
cues: Curl the bar in a smooth arc toward your chin.
Keep the cable taut at the bottom of every rep.
Keep the bar level, both ends rising together.

errors.error: Leaning back and swinging.
errors.fix: Reduce the load and keep the torso still; a staggered stance helps.

errors.error: Elbows travelling far forward, turning it into a front raise.
errors.fix: Keep the elbows close to your sides.

errors.error: Half reps at the bottom.
errors.fix: Straighten the arms fully each rep.

exercises.startingLoad: Start light (often the second or third plate, though stacks differ) and ramp up until 12-15 reps leave 2-3 in reserve.
exercises.effort: 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] once past the first two weeks; failure is safe with a cable.
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 10-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). Cable stacks give smaller relative jumps than dumbbells; use an add-on weight if the machine has one.
exercises.regression: Lighter load, or one arm at a time with a D-handle, left first.

alternatives.why: Loads the biceps long; replaces this curl from week 17 of Phase 3.
Upper arm fixed on a pad; the Upper B curl in Phases 2 and 4.
Neutral grip that shifts work to the brachialis and brachioradialis.

exercises.whyChosen: Planned variation: [[phase:p3]] rotates curls on a schedule (cable for 16 weeks, then incline dumbbell) rather than at random, the kind of variation a systematic review found can help without blunting progress [@Kassiano2022_variationSR]. The cable's small steps suit isolation work, and its constant tension loads the whole range ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: Very low risk. Stand close enough that the stack does not pull you forward, and keep the lower back neutral with soft knees rather than leaning back.
exercises.mechanism: A low cable pulls along its line toward the pulley, so its lever arm about the elbow is already substantial with the arm straight, unlike a dumbbell, whose lever arm is near zero at the bottom (biomechanical reasoning). The biceps both flexes the elbow and turns the palm up, so an underhand grip lets it contribute fully; the brachialis flexes the elbow in any grip (general anatomy).
exercises.evidence: Resistance-profile differences seem to matter little: cable and dumbbell lateral raises grew the deltoid equally [@Larsen2025_lateralRaiseDBvsCable], and machines versus free weights show no hypertrophy difference ([[term:smd|SMD]] -0.055) [@Haugen2023_freeVsMachineMeta]. Curls grew the elbow flexors about twice as much as rows (11.1% vs 5.2%) [@Mannarino2021_curl_vs_row]. Concentrating on squeezing the biceps (internal focus) gave more elbow-flexor growth than an external focus in one RCT (12.4% vs 6.9%) [@Schoenfeld2018_attentionalFocusHypertrophy], so on curls both kinds of cue are reasonable.

exercises.name: Hammer curl
exercises.summary: A dumbbell curl with your palms facing each other throughout, like swinging a hammer. The neutral grip shifts work toward the brachialis (beneath the biceps) and the brachioradialis (the large forearm muscle near the elbow), adding thickness to the upper arm and forearm. It is the Upper B curl in [[phase:p3]] (10-15 reps, 60 s rest).
setup: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, arms at your sides, palms facing your thighs.
Feet hip-width, knees soft, trunk lightly braced.
execution: Curl one dumbbell, starting with the left, or both together, in about 1 s, palm facing in and elbow at your side.
Stop when the forearm is near vertical and pause briefly.
Lower over 2-3 s to a straight arm. If alternating, finish the left rep before starting the right.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out on the curl, in on the way down.
cues: Lift the dumbbell like a hammer, thumb leading.
Keep the dumbbell handle vertical the whole way.
Move the dumbbell straight up beside your body, not across it.

errors.error: Swinging with the hips and back.
errors.fix: Use lighter dumbbells; stand with your back against a wall if needed.

errors.error: Curling across the body toward the opposite shoulder.
errors.fix: Lift straight up in front of the same shoulder.

errors.error: Short range at the bottom.
errors.fix: Straighten the arm fully each rep.

exercises.startingLoad: Usually a little heavier than your other curls: 7.5-10 kg per hand is a common start (practical convention), adjusted so 12-15 reps leave 2-3 in reserve.
exercises.effort: 0-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] after the first two weeks; stop at 0 RIR rather than failing a rep, since the programme keeps [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] for machines and cables ([[dec:D07]]).
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 10-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]); move up a dumbbell step when all sets reach 15.
exercises.regression: Lighter dumbbells, a seated hammer curl, or a rope hammer curl on a low cable.

alternatives.why: With a rope attachment it becomes a cable hammer curl.
Underhand curl with a long-length biceps emphasis.

exercises.whyChosen: A different grip shifts the load to different elbow flexors; a systematic review found that variation aimed at a different muscle or region can add growth, unlike random rotation [@Kassiano2022_variationSR]. It also builds grip and forearm strength that helps with pull-ups and carries (inference) ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: Low risk. Stop and reduce the load for pain on the outer elbow, which gripping work can provoke ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: The biceps brachii is also the forearm's main supinator, and with the palm facing in it pulls from a less favourable position, so the brachialis (which flexes the elbow in any grip) and the brachioradialis (strongest as a flexor with the forearm in neutral) take a larger share (general anatomy). Regional growth with this grip was not measured in the sources reviewed.
exercises.evidence: No trial located compares hammer curls with other curls for growth. Direct elbow-flexion work grew the elbow flexors about twice as much as rows (11.1% vs 5.2%) [@Mannarino2021_curl_vs_row], although in novices compound pulling alone also produced growth (6.5% vs 7.0% with added curls over 10 weeks) [@Gentil2013_singlejoint_addon]. Individual responses vary widely (biceps size changes from -2% to +59% in one study) [@Hubal2005_variability].

exercises.name: Dead bug
aliases: Supine opposite arm and leg reach
exercises.summary: Lying on your back with arms and legs raised, you slowly extend one arm and the opposite leg while keeping your lower back still against the floor. It teaches [[term:bracing|bracing]], holding the trunk stiff while the limbs move, which is the trunk's job in squats, rows, carries and martial arts. It is the core exercise in technique session A ([[phase:p0]], 6 per side) and in Full body A for weeks 1-6 of [[phase:p1]] (6-8 per side, 45 s rest).
setup: Lie on your back, knees bent 90 degrees above your hips, shins parallel to the floor, arms pointing straight at the ceiling.
Tighten your abdominals as if bracing for a light poke in the stomach, so your lower back rests gently on the mat; keep breathing.
The non-moving leg stays bent at 90 degrees. Straight-leg variants are limited by your tight hamstrings and are not needed.
execution: Exhale slowly as you lower the left leg (straightening it) and the right arm (back past your head) toward the floor over 3-4 s.
Stop just above the floor, or earlier if your lower back starts to lift off the mat; pause 1 s.
Return over 2 s and repeat with the right leg and left arm. Each pair is one rep per side; start every set with the left leg.
exercises.breathing: Exhale as the limbs extend, inhale as they return. The long exhale helps keep the ribs down and the lower back on the mat.
cues: Reach your heel toward the far wall.
Reach your hand toward the wall behind your head.
Keep the mat touching your lower back the whole time.
Move slowly enough to count every second.

errors.error: Lower back arching off the floor as the leg lowers.
errors.fix: Stop the leg higher until you can keep contact, then extend the range gradually.

errors.error: Holding the breath.
errors.fix: Exhale through each extension; if you cannot breathe while braced, the level is too hard.

errors.error: Rushing the reps.
errors.fix: 3-4 s out, 2 s back.

exercises.startingLoad: Body weight. If you cannot keep your lower back down through the full movement, move the legs only (arms stay up) or tap the heel down with the knee still bent.
exercises.effort: End each set while technique is still perfect, 2-3 reps before your back would lift; this is a control drill, not an endurance test.
exercises.progression: From 6 to 8 per side, then slower lowering (5 s), then holding a light plate or dumbbell in the hands. After week 6 of [[phase:p1]] the [[ex:cable-crunch]] takes its place.
exercises.regression: Legs only, or heel taps with the knees bent.

alternatives.why: Anti-extension hold on forearms and toes.
Anti-rotation bracing drill; the core exercise in Full body B.

exercises.whyChosen: A safe first core exercise for a novice training alone: it teaches bracing and breathing with no external load, is easy to regress, and puts no strain on the lower back ([[dec:D08]]). The bracing learned here carries into every loaded lift (practical convention).
exercises.safety: Very low risk. Stop if you feel pain in the lower back.
exercises.mechanism: When the leg lowers, the hip flexors (psoas attaches to the lumbar spine) pull the pelvis into anterior tilt and the lumbar spine toward extension. The abdominals must resist that pull to keep the spine still, an anti-extension task performed largely as an [[term:isometric|isometric contraction]] (functional anatomy). Moving opposite limbs adds a small rotational challenge.
exercises.evidence: In athletes, trunk-muscle training improved maximal strength ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.39) and local muscular endurance (SMD 1.29) versus active controls [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta]. In 1141 soldiers, a core-stabilisation programme and a sit-up programme gave similar injury rates [@Childs2010_situpVsCoreRCT]. An external focus on the movement's effect improves motor learning (retention g 0.58) [@Chua2021_externalFocusMA].

exercises.name: Plank (long-lever progression)
exercises.summary: Holding a straight body on forearms and toes. You already hold 60 s, so longer holds add little; this entry uses harder versions instead: the hardstyle (RKC) plank, maximal whole-body tension for 10-20 s, and the long-lever plank with the elbows ahead of the shoulders. It is not in the regular sessions: use it as a substitute for the dead bug or ab wheel, and for the optional plank test ([[ex:test-plank]]).
setup: Forearms on the mat with elbows under the shoulders (standard) or 10-20 cm ahead of them (long-lever).
Legs straight, feet hip-width, body in a straight line from head to heels.
Hardstyle: make fists and brace hard before lifting the knees.
execution: Hardstyle: squeeze glutes, thighs and abdominals as hard as you can and pull the elbows and toes toward each other without moving them; hold 10-20 s, rest 30-45 s, repeat 3-5 times.
Long-lever: move the elbows forward until the hold becomes hard by 20-30 s.
End the hold at the first sag of the hips or arch of the back.
exercises.breathing: Short, steady breaths behind the brace. In hardstyle holds the urge to hold your breath is strong; breathe in through the nose and out through pursed lips instead.
cues: Drag your elbows toward your toes across the floor.
Push the floor away with your forearms.
Tuck your belt buckle toward your chin.

errors.error: Hips sagging.
errors.fix: Squeeze the glutes, tuck the belt buckle toward the chin, and shorten the hold.

errors.error: Hips piked high.
errors.fix: Lower them until the body is straight; check with a mirror or a quick phone video.

errors.error: Chasing longer times.
errors.fix: Past 60 s, make the plank harder rather than longer (practical convention).

exercises.startingLoad: Body weight: 3-5 hardstyle holds of 10 s, or a long-lever plank with the elbows 10 cm ahead of the shoulders.
exercises.effort: Each hold should be very hard by its end but finish in good position; stop at the first loss of position.
exercises.progression: Hardstyle holds from 10 s to 20 s, then more holds; long-lever by moving the elbows further forward. The next step is the [[ex:ab-wheel]], a moving long-lever plank.
exercises.regression: Standard plank, or a plank from the knees.

alternatives.why: Anti-extension on your back; easier to control.
Dynamic, harder anti-extension.
Trains the sides of the trunk instead.

exercises.whyChosen: Your 60-s plank is a useful baseline but at that level a weak stimulus, so short, harder versions keep the anti-extension demand high (practical convention). Direct core work will not remove belly fat: six weeks of abdominal exercise left abdominal fat and waist circumference unchanged [@Vispute2011_absSpot], and in limb studies local training did not reduce local fat (g -0.03) [@RamirezCampillo2022_spotMeta]; waist fat falls with whole-body [[term:energy-balance|energy balance]] ([[sci:sci-energy]]).
exercises.safety: Very low risk. Lower-back discomfort during a hold means the position has slipped: reset or stop. Very high-tension holds with breath-holding raise blood pressure, so keep breathing (inference).
exercises.mechanism: Gravity pulls the trunk toward the floor, which would extend the lumbar spine; the abdominal wall resists with an [[term:isometric|isometric contraction]]. Moving the elbows forward lengthens the lever between your support and the trunk's centre of mass, so the same body weight creates a larger extension moment (basic mechanics). Hardstyle tension recruits many [[term:motor-unit|motor units]] for a short time instead of relying on endurance (inference).
exercises.evidence: Trunk training improves maximal strength and local muscular endurance in athletes ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.39 and 1.29) [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta]. In a matched trial, compound lifts without direct abdominal work still increased rectus abdominis size [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT], so rows, squats and presses already train the trunk. No trial located compares plank variants.

exercises.name: Side plank
exercises.summary: Holding your body straight on one forearm and the side of one foot. It trains the obliques and quadratus lumborum to resist side-bending, and the gluteus medius of the lower leg to hold the hips up. It is not in the regular sessions: use it as a substitute for the Pallof press or suitcase carry, or as extra work for the left side while your left-leg balance lags.
setup: Lie on your left side with the left elbow directly under the left shoulder, forearm flat on the mat. Left side first, then right.
Knees-bent version: knees bent 90 degrees and stacked. Full version: legs straight, top foot in front of the bottom foot for balance.
execution: Lift the hips until the body forms a straight line from head to knees (bent version) or head to feet.
Hold 20-30 s with steady breathing, then lower under control.
Switch sides and hold for the same time.
Harder: lift the top leg a few centimetres, or rest a light plate on the top hip.
exercises.breathing: Steady breathing throughout the hold; no breath-holding.
cues: Push the floor away with your forearm.
Lift your top hip toward the ceiling.
Keep your body in line with the edge of the mat.

errors.error: Hips sagging toward the floor.
errors.fix: Shorten the hold or use the knees-bent version.

errors.error: Hips rolling forward or back.
errors.fix: Line up shoulders, hips and feet along the edge of the mat; check in a mirror.

errors.error: Shoulder shrugged up toward the ear.
errors.fix: Push the floor away with the forearm.

exercises.startingLoad: Body weight; use the knees-bent version until a straight-leg hold of 20 s per side is steady.
exercises.effort: Finish each hold with 5-10 s still in reserve and the position intact. The left side sets the time; match it on the right.
exercises.progression: Build from 20 s to 45 s per side; then a raised top leg or a plate on the hip; then the loaded, walking version, the [[ex:suitcase-carry]].
exercises.regression: Knees-bent side plank, or an incline side plank with the forearm on a bench.

alternatives.why: Loaded, walking anti-side-bending.
Anti-rotation on a cable; the Full body B core exercise.
Front-on anti-extension hold.

exercises.whyChosen: Anti-side-bending completes the trunk mix of anti-extension, anti-rotation and flexion work (practical convention). On the left side it loads the left hip abductors, the muscles that keep the pelvis level when you stand on your left leg, the side that balances worse; whether that improves balance is untested (inference; see [[dec:D28]]).
exercises.safety: Very low risk. If the supporting shoulder hurts, use the knees-bent or incline version.
exercises.mechanism: Gravity pulls the hips toward the floor, which would bend the trunk sideways; the obliques and quadratus lumborum on the lower side resist isometrically. The gluteus medius of the bottom leg lifts and holds the pelvis, the same job it does when you stand on one leg (functional anatomy).
exercises.evidence: No trial located isolates the side plank. Trunk training as a whole improves maximal strength and local muscular endurance in athletes ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.39 and 1.29) [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta], and stabilisation-style programmes gave injury rates similar to sit-up programmes in soldiers [@Childs2010_situpVsCoreRCT].

exercises.name: Pallof press
exercises.summary: Side-on to a cable, you press a handle straight out from your chest and hold it there while the cable tries to twist you toward the machine. It trains the obliques and deep abdominals to resist rotation, the trunk's job in carrying, punching and changing direction. It is the core exercise in technique session B ([[phase:p0]], 8 per side) and Full body B ([[phase:p1]], 8-10 per side, 45 s rest).
setup: Set the pulley at chest height with a D-handle; a band anchored at chest height also works.
Stand or half-kneel side-on with the machine on your left first, holding the handle in both hands at the centre of your chest; step away until there is tension.
Half-kneeling: kneel on the knee nearer the machine with the other foot forward (practical convention). Standing: feet hip-width, knees soft.
Brace and square your hips and shoulders to the front.
execution: Press the handle straight out from your chest in 1-2 s until the arms are straight.
Hold 2-3 s without letting the hands drift toward the machine.
Bring the handle back to the chest over 1-2 s and repeat.
Do all reps with the machine on your left, then turn round.
exercises.breathing: Exhale as you press out, keep breathing through the hold, inhale as the handle returns.
cues: Press the handle straight out toward the wall in front of you.
Keep the handle on an imaginary rail in the middle of your body.
Keep your belt buckle pointing at the wall ahead.

errors.error: Rotating toward the machine.
errors.fix: Reduce the load; the handle must stay centred.

errors.error: Leaning away from the cable to resist it.
errors.fix: Stay vertical; the trunk muscles, not a lean, should hold you.

errors.error: Ribs flaring and lower back arching as the arms extend.
errors.fix: Exhale as you press and keep the ribs down.

exercises.startingLoad: The lightest or second-lightest setting; increase only when every rep stays centred for the full hold.
exercises.effort: Controlled reps with a steady hold; end the set about 2 reps before the handle starts to drift.
exercises.progression: Add load in small steps, then lengthen the hold to 5 s, then use a narrower standing stance. Reps follow [[term:double-progression|double progression]] within 8-10 per side ([[rule:double-progression]]).
exercises.regression: Lighter cable or band, a shorter hold, or the half-kneeling position.

alternatives.why: Anti-side-bending on the floor with no equipment.
Loaded anti-side-bending while walking.
Simpler bracing drill.

exercises.whyChosen: Anti-rotation work trains the bracing you need for lifting and for the twisting and stopping forces in martial arts and agility work (inference). It is easy to learn, puts no flexion load on the spine, and its load is easy to control alone ([[dec:D08]]).
exercises.safety: Very low risk. If your back aches during the hold, lighten the load; stop for pain ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: The cable pulls on your hands at a distance from your spine, creating a rotational moment. Pressing the hands away from the chest lengthens that lever, so the torque rises without any change in load (basic mechanics). The obliques work as diagonal pairs (the external oblique of one side with the internal oblique of the other), together with the transversus abdominis, to keep the trunk from turning: [[term:isometric|isometric]] work.
exercises.evidence: No trial located compares anti-rotation exercises with others for performance or injury in healthy adults. Trunk training in general improved maximal strength ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.39), sprinting (0.66) and change of direction (0.70) in athletes [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta]; that a stiffer trunk transmits force better is a hypothesis those trials did not test. Local trunk work did not reduce belly fat in a small trial [@Vispute2011_absSpot].

exercises.name: Cable crunch
exercises.summary: Kneeling below a high pulley with a rope held beside your head, you curl your ribs toward your pelvis against the cable. It is loaded spinal flexion, the most direct way to train the rectus abdominis (the 'six-pack' muscle) progressively, like any other lift. It replaces the dead bug in Full body A from week 7 of [[phase:p1]] (10-15 reps, 45 s rest).
setup: Set the pulley high and attach a rope. Kneel facing the machine, about a forearm's length away.
Hold the rope ends beside your forehead or ears, elbows bent.
Sit the hips slightly back with thighs near vertical; the hips stay at this angle throughout.
execution: Curl the trunk down in 1-2 s, bringing the elbows toward the mid-thighs by rounding the spine, ribs toward pelvis, not by bending at the hips.
Pause 1 s at the bottom.
Return over 2-3 s until the spine is long and the abdominals feel stretched; do not let the stack yank you upright.
exercises.breathing: Breathe out forcefully as you curl down, in as you rise.
cues: Bring the rope down toward the floor in front of your knees.
Keep your hips over your knees; only the rope and your chest move.
Keep the stack hovering at the top of each rep.

errors.error: Hinging at the hips, sitting back toward the heels instead of curling the spine.
errors.fix: Keep the hips still and think ribs to pelvis.

errors.error: Pulling with the arms.
errors.fix: Keep the rope fixed beside your head; the trunk moves it.

errors.error: Load so heavy that reps become jerky.
errors.fix: Lighten it until each rep is smooth and you feel the abdominals rather than the hip flexors.

exercises.startingLoad: Start light and ramp up; the abdominals are often stronger than expected, so taking a few sets to find a 10-15-rep load is normal.
exercises.effort: 1-2 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] once established. Failure is safe on the cable, but stop rather than grind reps that you feel in the lower back.
exercises.progression: [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] in 10-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). Keep loaded flexion modest: about 4-8 hard sets per week across all crunch-type exercises (practical inference).
exercises.regression: Lighter load, a floor crunch, or the [[ex:dead-bug]] if flexion bothers your back.

alternatives.why: Body-weight flexion from a bar; the Lower A core exercise in Phases 2 and 4.
No spinal flexion; use it if crunching provokes back symptoms.

exercises.whyChosen: Loaded flexion is the most direct way to overload the rectus abdominis, and the cable makes it progressive ([[dec:D08]]). Whether direct work adds abdominal muscle beyond what compound lifts provide is untested, so the dose stays modest. It will not reduce belly fat: six weeks of abdominal exercise left abdominal fat and waist circumference unchanged [@Vispute2011_absSpot]; that depends on whole-body [[term:energy-balance|energy balance]].
exercises.safety: Intervertebral discs are most swollen with fluid, and stiffest in bending, in roughly the first hour after waking, which is why loaded spinal flexion is conventionally kept out of the early morning (practical convention). You train about an hour after waking and this exercise comes at the end of the session, so keep it there rather than moving it to the start. Stop if it provokes back pain ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: The rectus abdominis runs from the lower ribs and sternum to the pubis, so shortening it flexes the spine; kneeling with fixed hips stops the hip flexors from taking over. The case against flexion exercise comes mainly from pig spines that herniated after up to 86,400 loaded flexion cycles in the laboratory [@Callaghan2001_porcineFlexion]; 3 sets of 15 is 45 cycles, roughly 1/1900 of that, with days of recovery in between (inference).
exercises.evidence: Soldiers on a sit-up-based programme had injury rates similar to those on core stabilisation (n = 1141), although among those with low-back injuries the sit-up group lost more work days (8.3 vs 4.2) [@Childs2010_situpVsCoreRCT], and low-quality evidence finds that lumbar flexion during lifting is not a risk factor for back pain [@Saraceni2020_lumbarFlexionMeta]. Compound lifts alone increased rectus abdominis size in trained men [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT]; no trial has measured how much direct crunching adds.

exercises.name: Hanging knee raise (to leg raise)
exercises.summary: Hanging from a bar, or supported on a captain's chair, and raising your knees toward your chest, curling the pelvis up at the top. The hip flexors lift the legs; the abdominals do the curl. It is the core exercise in Lower A in [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p4]] (8-15 reps, 60 s rest), and it doubles as grip work.
setup: Captain's chair (the place to start): back against the pad, forearms on the elbow pads, hands on the handles, legs hanging.
Bar: box underneath, hands and bar dry, overhand grip at shoulder width; hang with the shoulders gently engaged rather than fully relaxed.
Legs together and still before the first rep.
execution: Raise the knees toward the chest in 1-2 s.
At the top, curl the pelvis up so the hips tilt backward and the knees rise a little further; pause 1 s. This curl is the abdominal part of the rep.
Lower over 2-3 s to straight hips without swinging.
Straight-leg raises are the advanced version. Your tight hamstrings limit them, so keep the knees bent and straighten the legs only as far as you can without the knees bending back (inference).
exercises.breathing: Breathe out as you raise, in as you lower.
cues: Raise your knees toward the bar.
Curl your belt buckle up toward the bar at the top.
Lower your feet slowly back to a point under the bar.

errors.error: Swinging to lift the legs.
errors.fix: Pause at the bottom of every rep and slow the lowering; use the captain's chair if swinging persists.

errors.error: Lifting only the thighs without curling the pelvis.
errors.fix: Finish each rep by tilting the pelvis up.

errors.error: Grip failing before the abdominals.
errors.fix: Use the captain's chair, or straps on the bar, and train grip separately with carries.

exercises.startingLoad: Body weight on the captain's chair. Move to the bar when you can do 15 controlled reps on the chair.
exercises.effort: 1-3 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]. Reps that turn into swings do not count.
exercises.progression: Captain's chair, then hanging knee raise, then knees higher (toward the bar), then straight-leg raises to the height your hamstrings allow; within each stage use [[term:double-progression|double progression]] in 8-15 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). Later, a light dumbbell held between the feet (practical convention).
exercises.regression: Captain's chair knee raise, or a reverse crunch lying on a bench.

alternatives.why: Loaded flexion with no grip demand.
Floor-based trunk work with no hanging or spinal flexion.

exercises.whyChosen: It trains the abdominals and hip flexors together, needs only a bar, and doubles as grip and hanging practice for pull-ups ([[dec:D08]]). It counts toward the modest weekly flexion dose of about 4-8 hard sets (practical inference).
exercises.safety: Use a box to get on and off the bar. Sweaty hands at midday make grip fail without warning, so dry them and the bar between sets, and use the captain's chair when your grip is already tired. Stop for lower-back pain ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: Raising the thighs is hip flexion by the iliopsoas and rectus femoris; the rectus abdominis works most when the pelvis tilts backward and the lumbar spine flexes at the top. Because the psoas attaches to the lumbar spine, lifting the legs without that curl pulls the lower back toward extension (functional anatomy), which is why the pelvic curl matters.
exercises.evidence: No trial located compares hanging raises with other abdominal exercises. Trunk training improves maximal strength ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.39) and local muscular endurance (1.29) in athletes [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta]. A sit-up-based programme did not raise injury rates compared with core stabilisation in soldiers [@Childs2010_situpVsCoreRCT]; the main evidence against flexion exercise comes from pig spines put through tens of thousands of loaded cycles [@Callaghan2001_porcineFlexion].

exercises.name: Ab-wheel rollout
exercises.summary: Kneeling with your hands on a wheel, you roll forward until your body is nearly flat, then pull yourself back. It is a moving long-lever plank: the abdominals stop the lower back sagging into extension while the lats pull the arms back under you. It is the core exercise in Lower A in [[phase:p3]] (6-12 reps, 60 s rest).
setup: Kneel on a mat or folded towel with your hands on the wheel handles below your shoulders.
Face a wall about 60-90 cm from the wheel so it stops you at a range you can control; move further from it as you improve.
Tuck the pelvis slightly and brace, ribs down.
execution: Roll forward over 2-3 s, hips and shoulders moving together, until the wheel touches the wall or you reach the furthest point you can hold without the lower back sagging.
Pause briefly.
Pull the wheel back toward your knees in 1-2 s by pressing it down into the floor, keeping the trunk straight.
exercises.breathing: Exhale slowly as you roll out, inhale briefly at the far point, exhale as you pull back.
cues: Push the wheel away along a straight line on the floor.
Press the wheel down into the floor to pull it back.
Keep your belt buckle tucked toward your chin.

errors.error: Lower back sagging at the far end.
errors.fix: Shorten the range with the wall; this sag is the main thing to avoid.

errors.error: Hips staying back (piking) so only the arms move.
errors.fix: Let hips and shoulders travel forward together.

errors.error: Increasing the range too quickly.
errors.fix: Move further from the wall only when every rep at the current range is clean (practical convention).

exercises.startingLoad: Body weight from the knees with a short range: 2-3 sets of 6 with 2-3 reps in reserve.
exercises.effort: End each set 1-2 reps before the lower back would start to sag; losing position ends the set, not muscle failure.
exercises.progression: Range first (start further from the wall), then full kneeling rollouts to nearly flat, then a slower 4 s roll-out. Within each stage, [[term:double-progression|double progression]] in 6-12 reps ([[rule:double-progression]]). Standing rollouts are far harder and not needed for your goals (practical convention).
exercises.regression: A long-lever [[ex:plank]], a shorter range, or rollouts with an exercise ball under the forearms.

alternatives.why: Static version; the long-lever plank bridges to the wheel.
The easiest anti-extension drill.

exercises.whyChosen: The ab wheel is the most demanding anti-extension exercise in the trunk mix and progresses beyond the 60-s plank you can already hold ([[dec:D08]]). It loads the abdominals hard without spinal flexion, complementing the crunch-type work elsewhere in the programme.
exercises.safety: The main risk is letting the lower back sag at the far end, which loads it in extension; the wall stop prevents this when you train alone. Kneel on padding. Stop for any lower-back pain ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: As the wheel moves forward, the horizontal distance between your knees, the pivot, and the trunk's centre of mass grows, so the extension moment on the spine rises steeply (basic mechanics). The abdominals resist it isometrically, and on the way back the lats (extending the shoulder) and abdominals pull the body back over the knees. The roll-out is a controlled lowering, much like an [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] phase.
exercises.evidence: No trial located compares rollouts with other trunk exercises. Trunk training improves maximal strength and local muscular endurance in athletes ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.39 and 1.29) [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta]. Local exercise did not reduce local fat in a small abdominal-exercise trial or in a meta-analysis of limb studies [@Vispute2011_absSpot; @RamirezCampillo2022_spotMeta].

exercises.name: Farmer's carry
exercises.summary: Walking with a heavy dumbbell in each hand. It trains grip, the upper trapezius and the whole trunk as they hold you upright under load, with almost no technique to learn. It is the core exercise in Lower B in [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p4]] (30-40 m per set, 60 s rest).
setup: Choose a clear, straight path of 15-20 m. Midday is often a quieter time in commercial gyms (inference), but check the floor is free and let people nearby know you will be walking.
Your hamstrings are tight, so lift the dumbbells from the floor with a squat-style pick-up (knees bent, hips back, chest up, back flat), or take them from a bench or the bottom of the rack.
Grip the middle of the handles; stand tall with shoulders level and arms straight.
execution: Walk with short, quick steps, looking ahead.
Keep the dumbbells still and off your legs.
Turn with small steps at the end of the path, or set the dumbbells down and pick them up facing the other way.
Set them down at the end with the same squat-style movement.
exercises.breathing: Short, steady breaths behind a light brace; no breath-holding for the whole walk.
cues: Walk tall, as if a string pulls your head toward the ceiling.
Crush the handles.
Keep the dumbbells still at your sides.
Take short, quick steps along a straight line.

errors.error: Leaning forward or to one side.
errors.fix: Stand tall; reduce the load.

errors.error: Long, slow strides that set the weights swinging.
errors.fix: Use shorter, quicker steps.

errors.error: Lifting from the floor with straight legs.
errors.fix: Bend knees and hips, or pick the weights up from a bench.

errors.error: Waiting until the grip opens and the weights drop.
errors.fix: Set them down as soon as the grip starts to go.

exercises.startingLoad: A pair you could carry for about 60 m before your grip gives; 15-20 kg per hand is a common start for an untrained man (practical convention). In Hevy, log the load per hand and the distance.
exercises.effort: End each set when your grip is close to failing or your posture starts to slip, whichever comes first, and set the dumbbells down under control.
exercises.progression: Add distance up to 40 m, then go up one dumbbell step and return to 30 m. A long-term marker is carrying your body weight in total (half per hand) for 30-40 m (practical convention).
exercises.regression: Lighter dumbbells, a shorter distance, or standing holds of 20-30 s.

alternatives.why: One-sided version with more anti-side-bending demand.
Floor-based trunk work if there is no space to walk.

exercises.whyChosen: Carries train grip, posture and trunk stiffness together and are easy to do safely alone ([[dec:D08]]). Grip strength from carries should also help pull-ups and heavy rows (inference).
exercises.safety: Clear the path, and set the dumbbells down rather than dropping them: weights falling on the person caused 65.5% of weight-training injuries seen in US emergency departments [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. Midday heat makes hands sweaty, so dry them and the handles before each set. Stop for back pain ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: Heavy loads at your sides compress the spine and make the trunk muscles, upper trapezius and forearm flexors work isometrically to keep you upright, the shoulders set and the handles gripped. Each step briefly puts you on one leg, so the hip abductors (gluteus medius) keep the pelvis level on every stride (functional anatomy).
exercises.evidence: No trial located tests carries specifically. In a matched trial, compound lifts without direct abdominal exercise still grew the rectus abdominis [@HernandezBelmonte2023_freeVsMachineRCT], consistent with whole-body loading training the trunk (inference). Trunk training improves maximal strength and local muscular endurance in athletes ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.39 and 1.29) [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta].

exercises.name: Suitcase carry (one-sided)
exercises.summary: Walking with one heavy dumbbell in one hand, like carrying a suitcase, while staying perfectly upright. The weight tries to bend you sideways, and the obliques and quadratus lumborum on the opposite side stop it. It is the core exercise in Lower B in [[phase:p3]] (30 m each side, 60 s rest).
setup: Clear a straight path of about 15 m.
Left side first here means the left side doing the work, so start with the dumbbell in your RIGHT hand; that loads your left trunk muscles and left hip. Then switch.
Pick the dumbbell up with a squat-style lift (knees bent, back flat), keeping your shoulders level as you stand. The free arm hangs relaxed; do not hold onto anything.
execution: Walk 30 m (15 m out, turn slowly, 15 m back) with shoulders level and trunk vertical.
Set the dumbbell down with a squat-style lowering.
Switch hands and walk the same distance.
exercises.breathing: Short, steady breaths behind a light brace.
cues: Keep both shoulders level, like carrying a tray.
Walk tall, as if a string pulls your head up.
Keep the dumbbell still beside your leg.
Take short, quick steps along a straight line.

errors.error: Leaning toward the weight.
errors.fix: Use a lighter dumbbell; shoulders stay level.

errors.error: Leaning away from the weight to counterbalance it.
errors.fix: Stay vertical; the trunk muscles, not a lean, should hold you upright.

errors.error: Turning quickly at the end of the path.
errors.fix: Turn in small steps, or set the weight down and pick it up facing the other way.

exercises.startingLoad: One dumbbell of about 12.5-20 kg (practical convention), the same for both sides. In Hevy, log the weight and the distance per side.
exercises.effort: End each side when your grip or level posture starts to go. The first side (weight in the right hand) sets the load and distance; match it with the left hand.
exercises.progression: Add one dumbbell step once 30 m per side is steady and level, working toward the weight of one of your farmer's-carry dumbbells.
exercises.regression: A lighter dumbbell, a shorter distance, a standing hold of 20-30 s per side, or the [[ex:side-plank]].

alternatives.why: Static floor version of the same anti-side-bending task.
Two-handed version; more grip and posture, less side-bending.
Anti-rotation on a cable if there is no space to walk.

exercises.whyChosen: Carrying on one side adds the anti-side-bending demand that a two-handed carry cancels out, completing the trunk mix in [[phase:p3]] ([[dec:D08]]). Each step also puts you briefly on one leg under an uneven load, a small balance challenge that suits your aim of improving left-leg stability (inference; see [[dec:D28]]).
exercises.safety: As for the farmer's carry: clear the path, dry your hands, and set the weight down rather than dropping it, since dropped weights cause most weight-training injuries seen in emergency departments [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. Stop for back pain ([[rule:pain]]).
exercises.mechanism: The hand holding the weight is not the side doing most of the work. With the weight in the right hand, the load pulls the trunk to the right, so the left obliques and left quadratus lumborum resist. When you stand on the left leg, the right-hand load also increases the turning force about the left hip, so the left gluteus medius works harder to keep the pelvis level (functional anatomy).
exercises.evidence: No trial located tests one-sided carries, and whether they improve single-leg balance is untested. Trunk training in general improves maximal strength and local muscular endurance in athletes ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.39 and 1.29) [@Saeterbakken2022_trunkTrainingMeta], and stabilisation-style programmes gave injury rates similar to sit-up programmes in soldiers [@Childs2010_situpVsCoreRCT].
